title: How life might have begun: hot vents, the RNA world and deep time

summary.text: Every living cell today comes from another living cell. So the first cell had no parent cell, and nobody saw how they began. Scientists have two main ideas about the place: hot vents on the sea floor, or warm pools on land. In this lesson you will test whether a soap skin can form in sea-salty water, which is one of the arguments between the two ideas. You will also fit the whole age of the Earth onto your own arm span.
summary.art: A child shaking a clear bottle of foamy water at a table, with two more bottles beside her, and behind her a faint drawing of tall white chimneys on a dark sea floor.

intro.hook: A hen comes from an egg, and the egg comes from a hen. Every cell comes from a cell. Follow that back far enough and you reach a first cell with no parent. Where could that cell have come from?
intro.text: Nobody knows the answer yet. But scientists do not just guess. They look for places on Earth where the chemistry of life could start without any living being, and they test each step in the laboratory. In this lesson you will meet two such places, and test one of the arguments yourself with soap, salt and water. You will also see why the question is so hard. It happened about four billion years ago, and you will measure how long ago that is.
intro.art: A row of pictures going back in time: a child, her mother, a small furry animal, a fish, a single round cell, and then a question mark beside a bubbling crack in rock.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a first cell needed: a skin, instructions that can be copied, and a steady supply of energy.
By the end I can describe a hydrothermal vent, and tell a black smoker from an alkaline vent.
By the end I can explain the RNA world idea, give one piece of evidence for it and one problem with it.
By the end I can use my results from the Salt Water Skin Test to explain one argument between the vent idea and the pool idea.
By the end I can work out a scale and place the big events of Earth's history on a model of deep time.
By the end I can explain how scientists work out what the ancestor of all living cells was like.
By the end I can say which parts of the story are known, which are ideas being tested, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: A hydrothermal vent is an opening in the sea floor where hot water comes out. The water was heated inside the rock below.
terms.example: The Kairei vent field lies nearly 2,500 metres down in the Indian Ocean. Hot water full of dissolved minerals pours out of chimneys there.
terms.art: A dark chimney of rock on the sea floor with shimmering hot water pouring from its top.

terms.meaning: A black smoker is a very hot vent near an undersea volcano. Its water can be hotter than 350 degrees Celsius and looks like black smoke.
terms.example: The black colour is tiny grains of metal minerals. They turn solid when the hot water meets the cold sea.
terms.art: A tall dark chimney with a thick black cloud billowing from the top into dark blue water.

terms.meaning: A liquid is alkaline when it is the opposite of sour, or acid. Soap water and baking soda water are alkaline.
terms.example: Turmeric turns red in alkaline soap water. Turmeric stays yellow in acid lemon juice.
terms.art: A yellow turmeric stain on paper with one red patch where soapy water has dripped on it.

terms.meaning: An alkaline vent is a warm vent whose water is alkaline. It is heated by sea water reacting with rock, not by a volcano.
terms.example: The Lost City vents in the Atlantic Ocean are alkaline vents. Their water is 40 to 90 degrees Celsius and their chimneys are white.
terms.art: Tall white chimneys like church spires rising from a dark sea floor, with no smoke.

terms.meaning: Chemosynthesis is making food using energy from chemicals. Plants use energy from light, which is called photosynthesis.
terms.example: Bacteria at vents make sugar using energy from hydrogen sulfide, the gas that smells of rotten eggs.
terms.art: A tiny rod-shaped bacterium taking in small molecules from vent water and building a sugar.

terms.meaning: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. Atoms are the tiny particles that everything is made of.
terms.example: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: A water molecule drawn as one large ball with two small balls attached.

terms.meaning: RNA is a long chain molecule made of four kinds of building blocks. They are called A, U, C and G for short. The order of the letters carries instructions.
terms.example: Your cells copy a piece of DNA into RNA, and then read the RNA to build a protein.
terms.art: A chain of beads in four colours, each bead marked A, U, C or G.

terms.meaning: A nucleotide is one building block of RNA or DNA. Each letter in the chain is one nucleotide.
terms.example: A chain of 10 RNA letters is made of 10 nucleotides joined in a row.
terms.art: One bead lifted out of a four-colour chain, shown large with three parts drawn inside it.

terms.meaning: A catalyst is something that makes a chemical change go much faster. The catalyst is not used up by the change.
terms.example: The enzymes in your saliva are catalysts. They start breaking down the starch in rice while you chew.
terms.art: Two small molecules being brought together on the surface of a larger folded molecule.

terms.meaning: A ribozyme is a piece of RNA that works as a catalyst. Most catalysts in cells are proteins, so this was a surprise.
terms.example: The part of the ribosome that joins amino acids into a protein is made of RNA. So the ribosome is a ribozyme.
terms.art: An RNA chain folded into a knot-like shape, cutting another chain in two.

terms.meaning: A membrane is the very thin skin around a cell. It is made of fatty molecules, and it decides what goes in and out.
terms.example: Every one of your cells has a membrane. It is about 10,000 times thinner than a sheet of paper.
terms.art: A round cell cut open, with the thin double skin around the edge drawn enlarged.

terms.meaning: A fatty acid is a molecule with a head that mixes with water and a long tail that stays away from water. Soap is made from fatty acids.
terms.example: Coconut oil and ghee are built from fatty acids. A soap maker turns them into soap.
terms.art: A tadpole-shaped molecule with a round head in water and a long tail pointing away from it.

terms.meaning: A protocell is a simple bubble with a skin of fatty molecules and other molecules inside. It is not alive. Scientists make protocells to study how cells might have begun.
terms.example: In laboratories, tiny fatty acid bubbles with RNA inside have been made to grow and split in two.
terms.art: A tiny round bubble with a thin skin and a short coloured chain floating inside.

terms.meaning: LUCA is short for the last universal common ancestor. LUCA was the population of early cells that every living being today descends from.
terms.example: A neem tree, a crow, a mushroom, the bacteria in curd and you all descend from LUCA.
terms.art: A family tree with one cell at the bottom and a tree, a bird, a mushroom, bacteria and a child at the tips.

terms.meaning: Deep time is the huge stretch of time in Earth's history. It is measured in millions and billions of years.
terms.example: The Earth is about 4,500 million years old. Humans like us have lived for about 0.3 million years.
terms.art: A very long ribbon stretching into the distance, with a tiny coloured mark at the near end labelled 'people'.

terms.meaning: A scale model shows something too big or too long to see, at a size we can handle. One unit on the model always stands for the same amount of the real thing.
terms.example: On a map, 1 centimetre may stand for 10 kilometres. On your arm span, 1 centimetre may stand for 36 million years.
terms.art: A child with arms stretched wide, a tape measure running from fingertip to fingertip.

terms.meaning: A hypothesis is an idea that explains something and can be tested. It is not yet known to be right.
terms.example: 'Life began at alkaline vents' is a hypothesis. So is 'life began in warm pools on land'.
terms.art: A notebook page with an idea written at the top and two test results below it, one ticked and one crossed.

explanations.definition: Scientists who study the start of life look for three things together: a skin, instructions that can be copied, and a steady supply of energy.
explanations.description: Every living cell today has three things. The first is a membrane, a thin skin that keeps the cell's molecules together and apart from the water outside. The second is a set of instructions, written in DNA and RNA, which the cell copies and hands on to their young. The third is a steady supply of energy and of building materials, because a cell must keep building and repairing all the time. Why does this make the start of life hard to explain? Because in cells today, each of the three depends on the other two. The instructions say how to build the skin. The skin holds the instructions. Both need energy. So scientists ask how each one could have begun without the others, and where on the young Earth all three could have come together. This is simplified. Real cells need many more things. But these three are where most of the research is done.
examples: A bacterium in curd has a membrane, DNA and RNA instructions, and takes energy from the sugar in milk.
A soap bubble has a skin but no instructions and no energy supply. So a bubble does not grow, repair or have young.
A flame has a steady supply of energy but no skin and no instructions. So a flame is not counted as alive either.
explanations.art: Three drawings side by side: a bubble labelled 'skin', a chain of letters labelled 'instructions', and a small flame labelled 'energy', with arrows joining all three.

explanations.concept: Hydrothermal vents: black smokers and alkaline vents
explanations.definition: A hydrothermal vent is an opening in the sea floor where water heated inside the rock comes out. Black smokers are very hot and acid. Alkaline vents are warm and alkaline.
explanations.description: Sea water seeps down into cracks in the sea floor. Inside the rock the water is heated, and it dissolves minerals from the rock. Hot water is lighter than cold water, so it rises and comes out again. There are two main kinds of vent. A black smoker forms near an undersea volcano, where hot melted rock lies close below. Its water can be hotter than 350 degrees Celsius, and it is acid. It does not boil, because the weight of the sea above presses on it. When the hot water meets the cold sea, metal minerals turn solid as tiny black grains. They build a dark chimney. An alkaline vent needs no volcano. Sea water reacts with a green mineral called olivine. Olivine is found in rock that comes from deep inside the Earth. The reaction itself gives out heat. It also makes hydrogen gas and makes the water alkaline. This reaction has a long name, serpentinisation, because the new rock it makes is called serpentine. The water comes out at 40 to 90 degrees Celsius and builds white chimneys of carbonate, the material of limestone and seashells.
examples: Black smokers were first seen in 1979 on the East Pacific Rise. The water measured about 380 degrees Celsius.
The Lost City vents in the Atlantic are alkaline vents. The tallest chimney, called Poseidon, is about 60 metres high, as tall as an 18-storey building.
In December 2024, Indian scientists from NCPOR in Goa and NIOT in Chennai took their first pictures of an active vent. It lies about 4,500 metres down in the Indian Ocean.
In the Hot Vent in a Jar test, hot coloured water rises out of a small bottle through cold water. Vent water rises for the same reason.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the sea floor showing cold water going down cracks, heating up, and coming out through a black chimney on one side and white chimneys on the other.

explanations.concept: Life at vents lives on chemicals, not on sunlight
explanations.definition: Chemosynthesis is making food using the energy in chemicals. At vents, bacteria and archaea do this, and the other animals there depend on them.
explanations.description: No sunlight reaches the deep sea floor, so no plant can grow there. Yet vents are crowded with life. The food makers at a vent are microbes: bacteria, and their look-alikes called archaea. They take chemicals from the vent water, such as hydrogen sulfide or hydrogen gas. They use the energy in those chemicals to build sugar from carbon dioxide. Everyone else at the vent feeds on these microbes, or keeps them inside their own body. A giant tube worm has no mouth and no gut. They are fed by billions of bacteria who live inside them. This is simplified in one way. Most vent animals and many vent microbes also use oxygen dissolved in the sea water. That oxygen was made by photosynthesis far above. So most vent life today is not completely cut off from the Sun. But some vent microbes need no oxygen at all. They live on hydrogen and carbon dioxide alone, and scientists think the earliest cells may have lived like them.
examples: Giant tube worms at Pacific vents grow longer than a tall adult human, and have no mouth. Bacteria inside them make their food.
The scaly-foot snail lives at vents in the Indian Ocean. Their foot is covered in scales that hold iron.
Inside the Lost City chimneys live archaea who feed on hydrogen and methane from the rock.
explanations.art: A cluster of tall white tube worms with red plumes beside a vent, with a zoom-in circle showing rod-shaped bacteria inside one worm.

explanations.concept: The alkaline vent idea: energy from a difference
explanations.definition: The alkaline vent idea says that life began inside the chimneys of alkaline vents. The energy came from the difference between the alkaline vent water and the acid sea.
explanations.description: First, a fact about cells today. Every cell you know of gets usable energy in the same odd way. The cell pushes tiny charged particles called protons to one side of a membrane. Protons are what make a liquid acid. The protons then flow back through a tiny turning protein, and that flow is used to make ATP, the molecule that carries energy in cells. Peter Mitchell, a British scientist, worked this out in 1961. So every cell lives on a difference in acid between two sides of a thin skin. Now the idea. In 1989 the British geologist Michael Russell suggested that such a difference existed on the young Earth before any cell. Scientists think the early sea was a little acid, because the air held much more carbon dioxide than now. Alkaline vent water is the opposite. Inside a vent chimney the two are kept apart by thin mineral walls full of tiny holes. Russell, the biologist William Martin and the biochemist Nick Lane argue that this natural difference could have driven the first chemistry of life. Hydrogen from the vent and carbon dioxide from the sea could have been joined into the first carbon molecules. The tiny holes could have held the molecules together, as a cell does. The idea is not proven. In laboratory tests, hydrogen and carbon dioxide have been joined this way only in small amounts.
examples: In the Acid Sea, Alkaline Vent test, baking soda water and lemon juice meet on turmeric paper. You see a sharp line where alkaline meets acid.
Your own cells make ATP by letting protons flow across a membrane inside each mitochondrion.
Russell described alkaline vents as a likely place for life to start in 1989. The Lost City vents were found 11 years later, in 2000.
explanations.art: A zoom into a white chimney wall full of tiny chambers, with alkaline water on one side, acid sea water on the other, and small arrows crossing the thin wall.

explanations.definition: The RNA world idea says that before cells had DNA and proteins, there was a stage when RNA did both jobs: carrying the instructions and doing the work.
explanations.description: In cells today, DNA stores the instructions and proteins do most of the work. But proteins are built by following the instructions in DNA, and DNA can be copied only with the help of proteins. So which came first? RNA offers a way out. RNA carries instructions in the order of four letters, as DNA does. And in 1982 Thomas Cech found an RNA that cut and joined itself with no protein helping. RNA can be a catalyst too. A year later Sidney Altman found another. Such RNAs are called ribozymes. So one kind of molecule can do both jobs. In 1986 Walter Gilbert named the idea 'the RNA world'. The best evidence is inside you. The ribosome is the part of every cell that builds proteins. When scientists worked out its exact shape, they found that the part doing the joining is RNA. Venki Ramakrishnan, who was born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, shared the 2009 Nobel Prize with Ada Yonath and Thomas Steitz for this work. There are real problems too. RNA is fragile and breaks up in hot water. Its building blocks are hard to make without cells. In 2009 John Sutherland's team made two of the four from simple chemicals, which helped. And nobody has yet shown an RNA that copies all of itself, again and again, without help. Scientists have made ribozymes that copy other short RNA chains, and they are getting closer.
examples: The ribosome in a rice plant, in a crow and in you has the same RNA core. All three inherited it from very early cells.
ATP, the energy-carrying molecule in every cell, is built from the RNA letter A. Many scientists see this as another trace of an RNA world.
In the game Copy or Crash, you find out why a long RNA chain is harder to copy without a mistake than a short one.

perspectives.explanation: RNA can store instructions and act as a catalyst, and the oldest machines in the cell are built around RNA. So an RNA stage is the simplest way to explain how instructions and workers began together.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think metabolism came first
perspectives.explanation: RNA is too fragile and too hard to make to be the first step. They think simple chains of chemical reactions, fed by energy at a vent, came first and RNA arose later inside them.

perspectives.who: Scientists who think RNA and small proteins began together
perspectives.explanation: Short chains of amino acids form easily and help RNA to hold its shape. In this view there was never a world of RNA alone.

explanations.art: One RNA chain shown twice: on the left stretched out as a row of letters, on the right folded into a shape that grips another molecule.

explanations.concept: The copying problem: more letters, more mistakes
explanations.definition: Every copy of a chain can have mistakes. The longer the chain, the more likely it is that a copy has at least one mistake.
explanations.description: Suppose a copier makes a mistake on about one letter in every six. A chain of 4 letters will often be copied perfectly. A chain of 12 letters almost never will. After a few rounds of copying, the long message is lost in mistakes. The German chemist Manfred Eigen pointed this out in 1971. It makes a puzzle for the RNA world. A good copier needs a long RNA chain, because a short chain cannot fold into a careful copying shape. But a long chain cannot be kept without a good copier. Scientists call this Eigen's paradox. A paradox is two things that both seem true but cannot both be true. There are several ideas for how early RNA got around it. Perhaps several short chains worked together. Perhaps a skin kept good copiers and their copies in the same bubble. Mistakes are not only a problem. A small number of mistakes is how new kinds of chain appear, so that some can work better than their parents. Too many mistakes lose the message. With no mistakes at all, nothing new can ever appear.
examples: In Copy or Crash, a 4-letter chain is copied with no mistake about half the time. A 12-letter chain manages this about one time in nine.
Your cells copy 3 billion DNA letters with very few mistakes. They use proteins that check each letter and fix errors.
When you copy a long phone number by hand, you are more likely to slip than with a short one.
explanations.art: A short chain and a long chain, each copied three times in a row, with the long chain's copies showing more and more red wrong letters.

explanations.concept: Skins that form by themselves, and the trouble with salt
explanations.definition: Fatty acid molecules in water line up by themselves into thin skins and hollow bubbles. Salt in the water can stop this. Scientists disagree about what that means for where life began.
explanations.description: A fatty acid molecule has a head that mixes with water and a long tail that stays away from water. Put many of them in water and they arrange themselves. The tails turn towards each other and the heads face the water. The result is a thin double layer, which can close up into a hollow bubble far too small to see. Nobody has to build it. Jack Szostak and other scientists have made such bubbles with RNA inside, and have seen them grow and split. These are protocells. Soap is made from fatty acids, so soap shows the same behaviour on a size you can see. The wall of a soap bubble is a thin film of water with soap molecules lined up on both faces. This is a model, not the same thing. A cell membrane is a double layer in water, and a bubble wall is a film in air. But both form because of the same head and tail. Now the trouble. Sea water holds salt, and the particles of salt pull fatty acids out of the water into solid specks. Then there are fewer left to make skins. You test this in the Salt Water Skin Test.
examples: In the Salt Water Skin Test, the same soap usually makes tall foam in plain water and much less in sea-salty water.
In 2018 David Deamer's team mixed fatty acids into hot spring water and into sea water. Bubbles formed in the spring water and not in the sea water.
In 2019 Sean Jordan and Nick Lane's team used a mixture of 12 fatty molecules. Bubbles did form in warm, salty, alkaline water.

perspectives.explanation: Fatty acid skins fall apart in sea water, so the first cells could not have formed in the sea. They needed fresh water, such as hot spring pools on land.

The earlier tests used only one or two kinds of fatty molecule. A vent would make a mixture, and a mixture forms skins well in warm, salty, alkaline water. So the salt argument does not rule out vents.

explanations.art: A zoom-in of tadpole-shaped molecules in water arranged in a double layer that curves round into a hollow ball.

explanations.concept: Warm pools on land: wet and dry, again and again
explanations.definition: The warm pool idea says that life began in small hot spring pools on land. The pools dried out and filled again many times, and drying pushed small molecules together into chains.
explanations.description: In 1871 Charles Darwin wrote to his friend Joseph Hooker that life might have started in 'some warm little pond'. The modern form of the idea comes from David Deamer and Bruce Damer. To join building blocks into a chain such as RNA, a molecule of water must be removed at each join. In the open sea that is hard, because there is water everywhere, and water tends to break such chains apart again. In a pool at the edge of a hot spring, the water dries up and comes back many times a day. Each time the pool dries, the molecules are crowded together on the rock and some join into chains. Each time the pool fills, fatty skins form and wrap up some of the chains. In Pune, Sudha Rajamani's laboratory at IISER tests such wet and dry cycles. Her team has shown that they help building blocks join, and that they change the fatty skins too. The pool idea has problems as well. The young Earth had little dry land. Strong ultraviolet light from the Sun reached the ground, because there was no ozone layer, and it breaks many molecules. Some scientists answer that the same light also drives useful reactions.
examples: In Drying Drops, salt and turmeric in a drop of water end up crowded in a ring when the drop dries.
When rasam boils down in the pan, the same salt is left in less water, so it tastes saltier. Drying crowds dissolved things together.
Hot springs rise today at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and at Yellowstone in the United States. Small pools at the edges of such springs dry out and fill again.
explanations.art: A small steaming pool on bare dark rock under a hazy sky, with a pale dried ring around the edge and a zoom-in showing small molecules joined into a chain.

explanations.concept: Where did life begin? The debate today
explanations.definition: Scientists do not agree on where life began. The two leading ideas are alkaline vents in the deep sea and warm pools on land.
explanations.description: Each idea explains some things well and others badly. Vents give a steady supply of energy and of hydrogen for millions of years, and they are sheltered from sunlight and from falling space rocks. The way all cells use protons fits the vent idea well. But a vent is surrounded by sea water, which tends to break chains apart and may stop fatty skins from forming. Pools join building blocks into chains easily and let fresh water skins form. But pools are small, short-lived and open to harsh sunlight. It is possible that neither is right, or that the steps happened in different places. It is also possible that we can never know for certain, because the Earth has destroyed almost all rocks older than 4 billion years. What scientists can do is test whether each step works. That is why the work is done step by step in laboratories.
examples: The game Vent, Pool or Both lets you sort 16 real findings by which idea each one supports.
Saturn's moon Enceladus has a salty ocean under ice. In 2017 scientists reported hydrogen gas in the jets that shoot from it, a sign of vents on its sea floor.
If life began in pools on land, an ocean moon with no dry land would be a poor place to look for life.

perspectives.who: Michael Russell, William Martin and Nick Lane
perspectives.explanation: Life began inside alkaline vents. The natural difference between vent water and sea water gave the energy, and all cells still use such a difference today.
Life began in hot spring pools on land. Wet and dry cycles joined building blocks into chains, and fatty skins formed in the fresh water.
The building blocks of RNA can be made on the Earth's surface from simple chemicals, with ultraviolet light from the Sun driving the reactions. That light does not reach the deep sea.
The evidence is not strong enough to choose. Different steps may have happened in different places, and the place may never be known for sure.

explanations.art: A split picture: on the left, white chimneys on a dark sea floor, and on the right, a steaming pool on bare land, with a question mark between them.

explanations.concept: LUCA: reading the ancestor from living cells
explanations.definition: LUCA is the last universal common ancestor, the early cells from whom all living beings today descend. Scientists work out what LUCA was like from what all living cells share.
explanations.description: No fossil of LUCA has been found. So how can anyone say what LUCA was like? The method is the one you use in a family. If you, your cousin and your second cousin all have the same rare family recipe, the simplest explanation is that one shared ancestor had that recipe and passed it down. Biologists do this with genes. A gene found in bacteria, in archaea and in us was most likely already in the ancestor of all three. This way they find that LUCA already had a membrane, DNA, RNA, ribosomes, the genetic code and the proton way of making ATP. So LUCA was a full cell, not the first life. Much had already happened before LUCA. In 2016 William Martin's team found 355 gene families that go back to LUCA. Those genes suggest a cell who lived without oxygen, in a hot place, feeding on hydrogen, as microbes at vents do. A study in 2024 estimated that LUCA lived about 4.2 billion years ago and had about 2,600 kinds of protein. Both studies are argued over, and the date is uncertain.
examples: In Find the Ancestor, you compare four living beings and work out which features their shared ancestor must have had.
The three RNA letters AUG mean 'start here' in a curd bacterium, a banana plant and a human. All inherited the code from LUCA.
The oldest fossils that almost all scientists accept are stromatolites in Western Australia, about 3.48 billion years old. LUCA is older than any known fossil.
explanations.art: A tree diagram with three big branches labelled bacteria, archaea and 'cells with a nucleus', all meeting at one cell at the base labelled LUCA.

explanations.concept: Deep time on a scale model
explanations.definition: A scale model of time uses a length to stand for years. Every centimetre stands for the same number of years, so you can see how long each stretch of history was.
explanations.description: The Earth is about 4,500 million years old. The number is easy to say and almost impossible to picture. A scale model helps. You choose a length, such as your arm span, and let it stand for all 4,500 million years. Then you divide. If your arm span is 125 centimetres, each centimetre stands for 4,500 divided by 125, which is 36 million years. Now every event has a place. To find it, divide how long ago the event was by 36. The American writer John McPhee described this model in 1981, in the book where he first used the words 'deep time'. He pointed out that all of human history fits in the very tip of a fingernail. A scale model also shows why the start of life is so hard to study. It lies near the far fingertip. Almost no rock that old is left on Earth.
examples: On an arm span of 125 centimetres, the dinosaurs died out less than 2 centimetres from the fingertip.
On the same arm span, the 5,000 years since people began to write are far thinner than a hair.
The universe is about 13,800 million years old. On the same scale, that would need a little more than three arm spans.
explanations.art: A child with arms stretched wide, coloured stickers along one arm and across her chest, and one tiny sticker at the very tip of a finger.

agreed.text: Every living cell today comes from another living cell.
agreed.evidence: Louis Pasteur showed in the 1860s that boiled broth stays free of microbes if dust is kept out. No one has ever seen a cell appear from non-living material.

agreed.text: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and life is at least 3.5 billion years old.
agreed.evidence: Meteorites and the oldest minerals are dated by the steady change of radioactive atoms. Layered fossils made by microbes, called stromatolites, are found in rocks 3.48 billion years old in Western Australia.

agreed.text: All living beings today descend from one population of early cells, called LUCA.
agreed.evidence: Every cell uses the same four DNA letters, almost the same genetic code, ribosomes with an RNA core, and ATP. So many shared features are best explained by one shared ancestor.

agreed.text: The small building blocks of life can form without living beings.
agreed.evidence: Stanley Miller made amino acids from simple gases with electric sparks in 1952. Amino acids are also found in meteorites, and John Sutherland's team made RNA building blocks from simple chemicals in 2009.

agreed.text: RNA can carry instructions and can also work as a catalyst.
agreed.evidence: Thomas Cech found the first ribozyme in 1982. The part of the ribosome that joins amino acids is made of RNA.

agreed.text: Fatty molecules form skins and bubbles in water by themselves.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see soap films form. Under microscopes, scientists see fatty acids form closed bubbles that can hold RNA, grow and split.

agreed.text: Nobody yet knows how or where life began.
agreed.evidence: No laboratory has made a living cell from non-living chemicals. Scientists who support vents and scientists who support pools publish evidence against each other's ideas every year.

challenging.claim: Life began inside alkaline vents on the sea floor.
challenging.who: Michael Russell, William Martin, Nick Lane and others, from 1989
challenging.for: Vents give steady energy for a very long time. All cells still make energy from a difference in acid across a membrane, as a vent chimney has naturally. LUCA's genes look like those of a vent microbe.
challenging.against: Sea water tends to break chains such as RNA apart, and salt can stop simple fatty skins from forming. Joining hydrogen and carbon dioxide has worked only weakly in laboratory vents.
challenging.context: This card is about one of the two leading ideas of where life began.

challenging.claim: Life began in warm pools on land that dried and filled again.
challenging.who: Charles Darwin in 1871, and David Deamer and Bruce Damer today
challenging.for: Drying joins building blocks into chains. Fatty skins form well in fresh spring water. Sunlight can drive the making of RNA building blocks.
challenging.against: The young Earth had little land. Pools are small and do not last. Ultraviolet light and falling space rocks made the surface a harsh place.
challenging.context: This card is about the other leading idea of where life began.

challenging.claim: RNA came first, before DNA and proteins.
challenging.who: Alexander Rich in 1962, then Carl Woese, Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel. Walter Gilbert named it the RNA world in 1986.
challenging.for: RNA can store instructions and act as a catalyst. The ribosome's working core is RNA.
challenging.against: RNA is fragile and hard to make. No RNA has yet been shown to copy all of itself without help.
challenging.context: This card is about which molecule of life came first.

challenging.claim: Chains of chemical reactions came first, and instructions came later.
challenging.who: Günter Wächtershäuser, Michael Russell and others
challenging.for: Simple reactions fed by vent chemicals need no fragile long chains. Some of the oldest reactions in cells can run on mineral surfaces without proteins.
challenging.against: Without instructions that are copied, it is hard to see how a set of reactions could improve over generations.
challenging.context: This card is about a view that disagrees with the RNA world idea.

challenging.claim: Life, or its building blocks, came to Earth from space.
challenging.who: An old idea, held today by a small number of scientists for life itself
challenging.for: Amino acids and other building blocks really are found in meteorites. So space did deliver some building blocks.
challenging.against: No living cell has ever been found in a meteorite. And even if life came from elsewhere, we would still have to explain how life began there.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that life did not begin on Earth.

challenging.claim: All life on the sea floor depends on food that sinks from the sunlit water above.
challenging.for: Plants need light, and no light reaches the deep sea. The deep sea floor that had been sampled held few animals.
challenging.against: In 1977 crowded communities of animals were found at vents. Colleen Cavanaugh showed that bacteria there make food from chemicals.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that was shown wrong when vents were discovered.

big_questions.q: A soap skin has no instructions. RNA has no skin. A vent has energy but neither. At what point would you call something alive?
big_questions.hint: Try listing what a thing must be able to do. Then test your list on a flame, a seed and a virus.

big_questions.q: In the Salt Water Skin Test, nobody built the foam. Can order appear without anyone making it?
big_questions.hint: Think of salt crystals, snowflakes and the hexagons in a honeycomb. Which had a maker and which did not?

big_questions.q: If nobody can go back and watch life begin, how can we ever claim to know how it happened?
big_questions.hint: A detective was not at the crime either. What kinds of evidence does a detective use?

big_questions.q: Life began once, about four billion years ago, and never again as far as we know. Why not again?
big_questions.hint: Think about who would eat any new beginnings today. Also think about how the air and sea have changed.

big_questions.q: On your arm span, people are a sliver at one fingertip. Does that make us less important, or the story more ours?
big_questions.hint: There is no right answer. Notice that every cell before you had to survive for you to be here.

big_questions.q: If we find living cells on Enceladus, how could we tell whether they are our relatives or began separately?
big_questions.hint: Think about what all Earth life shares: the same letters, the same code. Would strangers share them?

story.title: The City Nobody Was Looking For
story.note: This is a true story. The ship, the date, the people, the camera sled Argo, the dive in Alvin, the white towers and what heats them are all real. Gretchen Früh-Green's two short sentences in quotation marks are her own words, as she told them afterwards. The other spoken words, and what people were thinking in the control room, are imagined.
text: In December 2000, a research ship called Atlantis was working in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. Under the ship, far down in the dark, stood a mountain. The mountain is called the Atlantis Massif, and its top is still hundreds of metres below the waves.

The scientists on board had come to study the mountain's rock. Donna Blackman, who led the voyage, wanted to know how such a mountain had been pushed up from deep inside the Earth. Nobody on the ship was looking for hot vents.

There was a good reason for that. Everyone knew where vents were found. A vent needs heat, and the heat comes from melted rock under an undersea volcano. The nearest line of volcanoes was fifteen kilometres away. The mountain under the ship was old and cold.

The scientists could not go down themselves every day. So at night they lowered a sled of cameras called Argo on a long cable. Argo flew slowly above the mountain, and sent pictures up to a small crowded room on the deck. The scientists took turns to sit there in the dark and watch the screens.

On the night of the third of December, the first watch saw grey rock, pale mud and a few curious fish. At midnight the second watch took over, led by a geologist called Barbara John. Beside her sat Gretchen Früh-Green, who had come from Zurich in Switzerland. The grey rock went on sliding past.
Then something white came into the picture.
It was tall, and it had branches like fingers. More white shapes came out of the dark behind it. 'When I first saw them I thought they were corals,' Gretchen said later.

She looked again. Corals are animals, and these were not alive. They were spires and cones of pale rock, as fine and white as frost on a window. Some stood higher than the camera's lights could reach.
'Then I went and got Debbie,' she said.
Debbie was Deborah Kelley. She had spent years studying vents, and she had seen more of them than almost anyone on Earth. She came into the little room and stared at the screens.
They were chimneys. She was sure of that. But they were the wrong chimneys in the wrong place.

Every vent chimney she knew was dark, built from black grains of metal. These were white. Every vent she knew poured out water like thick smoke. Nothing here was smoking. And every vent she knew sat on top of a volcano. Here there was no volcano at all.
The room filled with people. Somebody asked the question that all of them were thinking. If there is no fire under this mountain, what is heating the water?
The next day, Debbie Kelley and Jeff Karson climbed into Alvin, a small submarine with room for three. Alvin sank down through the dark water. Then its lights found the towers.

There were many of them. The tallest stood sixty metres high, as tall as a building of eighteen floors. No one had ever seen a vent chimney so tall. Clear water shimmered out of the white walls, the way air shimmers over a hot road in May.
When the water was tested, it was warm, not scalding. And it was alkaline, like soapy water, where the water of every vent they knew was acid.

The answer to the question was in the mountain itself. The Atlantis Massif is made of a green rock from deep in the Earth. When sea water seeps into that rock, the rock and the water react. The rock swells and cracks, so more water gets in. And the reaction gives out heat.

So there was no fire to find. The rock and the sea were warming the water between them, and they had been doing so for at least thirty thousand years. The same reaction made the water alkaline. It also filled the water with hydrogen gas.
Inside the white walls, the scientists later found living microbes. They were feeding on that hydrogen.

Eleven years earlier, a geologist called Michael Russell had written that warm, alkaline vents ought to exist on the sea floor. He had never seen one, and neither had anyone else. He had also suggested that life itself might have started inside one.

Now there was a real one to study. And the green rock is not rare. When the Earth was young, far more of it lay open on the sea floor. Wherever it met the sea, it could have built warm white towers like these, with no volcano needed.
The scientists named the place Lost City. It stands on the Atlantis Massif, it was found from the ship Atlantis, and in the old Greek story Atlantis is a city lost under the sea.

Debbie Kelley was careful afterwards. Nobody could say that life began in towers like these, she told people. But she thought such places had very likely kept early life going. They are warm and steady, and they last for thousands of years.
Gretchen Früh-Green went on studying Lost City for many years. She had thought she was looking at coral. She had found a kind of place that no one had known was on the Earth.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn in this story is the question 'what is heating the water?' The scientists expected a volcano, because every vent known until then had one. The answer was that the rock and the sea water heat each other by reacting. That reaction, called serpentinisation, also makes the water alkaline and fills it with hydrogen. This is why alkaline vents matter for the start of life. They need only sea water and a common deep rock, so they could have been widespread on the young Earth. The story also shows how science often moves: by people noticing something that should not be there.
ask: Why was nobody on the ship looking for vents on that mountain?
Black smokers are heated by melted rock. What heats an alkaline vent?
Michael Russell said such vents should exist before anyone saw one. What does that tell you about a good idea in science?
The scientists found Lost City by accident. Was it luck, or something more than luck?
Debbie Kelley would not say that life began in such towers. Why do you think she was so careful?

games.title: Vent, Pool or Both? The evidence game
games.context: This is a card game about where life began. Each card gives one real finding. You decide whether it supports deep-sea vents, warm pools on land, or both.

printables.title: 16 evidence cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Every living cell makes ATP, the energy molecule, by letting protons flow across a membrane.
items.b: Vents. A vent chimney has a natural difference in protons across its thin walls, so cells may have started by using it.

items.f: In 2018, fatty acids formed bubbles in hot spring water, but not in sea water.
items.b: Pools. A first cell needs a skin, and simple skins formed in fresh water only.

items.f: In 2019, a mixture of 12 fatty molecules formed bubbles in warm, salty, alkaline water.
items.b: Vents. A mixture of molecules can make skins in vent-like water, so salt does not rule vents out.

items.f: When a drop of water dries, small building blocks are pushed together and some join into chains.
items.b: Pools. Pools on land dry and fill again. The deep sea never dries.

items.f: Chains such as RNA tend to break apart in water, more quickly when the water is hot.
items.b: Pools. A vent is always under water. A pool gives the chains dry spells.

items.f: The oldest genes shared by all cells look like the genes of microbes who feed on hydrogen and need no oxygen.
items.b: Vents. Alkaline vents give off hydrogen, and microbes like this live there today.

items.f: In the laboratory, ultraviolet light helps to make the building blocks of RNA from simple chemicals.
items.b: Pools. Ultraviolet light from the Sun reaches a pool on land. It does not reach the deep sea.

items.f: Strong ultraviolet light breaks many molecules, and the young Earth had no ozone layer to block it.
items.b: Vents. The deep sea floor is sheltered from ultraviolet light.

items.f: The Lost City vents have been active for at least 30,000 years.
items.b: Vents. Slow chemistry needs a place that stays the same for a very long time.

items.f: Many scientists think the young Earth was almost all ocean, with very little dry land.
items.b: Vents. With little land there would be few pools. But this is uncertain, so it is weak evidence.

items.f: Large rocks from space hit the surface of the young Earth far more often than today.
items.b: Vents. The deep sea floor was safer than the surface.

items.f: The walls of alkaline vent chimneys are full of tiny chambers.
items.b: Vents. Tiny chambers could keep molecules together, as a cell's skin does.

items.f: Amino acids form from simple gases with sparks, and they are found in meteorites.
items.b: Both. Building blocks from the air or from space could reach the sea and the land.

items.f: Signs of life 3.48 billion years old have been found in rocks that formed at hot springs on land.
items.b: Pools. It shows that very early life lived at land hot springs. It does not prove life began there.

items.f: The chemistry of every living cell happens in water.
items.b: Both. A vent and a pool are both full of water.

items.f: In laboratory vents, hydrogen and carbon dioxide have been joined into carbon molecules, but only in small amounts.
items.b: Vents, but weakly. The first step works a little. Nobody has shown that it works well enough.

printables.title: Score sheet: draw one row for each player
items: Good reasons given (one tally mark each)

rules: Shuffle the 16 cards. Put them in a pile with the finding side up.
On your turn, read the top finding aloud. Say 'vents', 'pools' or 'both', and give your reason.
Turn the card over and read the back. If your answer matches, keep the card.
If your reason was a good one, the other players give you one extra tally mark, even if your answer was different.
If your answer does not match, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
The game ends when the pile is empty, or after 20 minutes. The player with the highest total wins.
Playing alone: sort all 16 cards into three piles before you look at any back. Then check. Try to get 12 or more right.

setup.art: A pile of small cards on a table with the top card reading 'The Lost City vents have been active for at least 30,000 years', beside a pencil and a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Put the pile with the finding side up.

setup.art: A girl holding a card and speaking to her father, one finger raised as she gives a reason.
setup.caption: 2. Read the finding. Say vents, pools or both, and say why.

setup.art: The girl turning the card over to read the back, with three small piles of won cards beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them in a pile, finding side up. 4. Draw a score row for each player.
flow.say: Each card is one real finding. We will decide which idea it supports: vents, pools or both.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Put them finding side up. Draw a score row.
flow.context: This is the first step of Vent, Pool or Both. Here you set up the evidence cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a finding aloud. 2. Say vents, pools or both, with a reason. 3. Turn the card over and check. 4. Mark the score.
flow.say: Read the finding. Which idea does it support? Tell me your reason before you turn the card.
flow.kid: Read the card aloud. Say vents, pools or both. Give your reason. Then turn the card over.

ask.q: Could this finding fit the other idea as well? How?
good: Yes, if the vent idea is changed a little.
No, because the deep sea never dries out.

flow.parent: The reason matters more than the answer. Some cards can be argued both ways, and a child who argues well for the other side has understood the card.
flow.context: This is the main part of Vent, Pool or Both. Here you decide which idea each finding supports.

flow.do: 1. Count the scores. 2. Lay all the cards in two rows, one for vents and one for pools. 3. Ask which row is stronger, and what is still missing.
flow.say: Look at both rows. Which idea has the stronger evidence, in your opinion? What finding would change your mind?
flow.kid: Lay the cards in two rows. Which idea looks stronger to you? What would change your mind?

check.q: Drying pushes building blocks together into chains. Which idea does this support?
options: It proves life began in pools
check.why: Pools dry and fill again, and the deep sea never dries. So this finding supports pools. It does not prove anything alone, because one finding is one piece of evidence.

flow.context: This is the last step of Vent, Pool or Both. Here you weigh all the evidence together.

games.title: Copy or Crash: the copying mistake game
games.context: This is a dice game about copying RNA. You choose a short, medium or long chain and roll to see whether the copy has a mistake. It shows why the first RNA chains could not be long.

printables.title: Score sheet: draw these columns, and one row for each turn
items: Number of 1s rolled (each 1 is a copying mistake)

rules: You need one die, a pencil and the score sheet. Each player's RNA chain is copied once on every turn.
On your turn, choose your chain length: 4, 8 or 12 letters. Say it aloud before you roll.
Roll the die once for each letter. So roll 4, 8 or 12 times.
Every 1 you roll is a copying mistake. If you roll no 1s, the copy is perfect and you score the chain length: 4, 8 or 12 points.
If you roll even one 1, the copy does not work. You score 0 for that turn.
The first player to reach 24 points wins.
Second game: now you have a checker. Each time you roll a 1, roll that letter again once. Only a second 1 counts as a mistake.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to reach 24. Play once with no checker and once with the checker, and compare.

setup.art: A die, a pencil and a hand-drawn score sheet with five columns on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the score sheet.

setup.art: A girl holding up eight fingers to show her choice, with the die in her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Choose 4, 8 or 12 letters. Roll once for each letter.

setup.art: A die showing a 1 on the table, and the girl writing 0 on her score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Any 1 is a mistake. No 1s means you score the chain length.

flow.do: 1. Draw the score sheet. 2. Explain the rules. 3. Ask which chain length your child expects to score best over many turns, and why.
flow.say: A long chain scores more when the copy is perfect. Which length do you think will win over many turns? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw the score sheet. Guess which chain length will score best. Say why.
flow.parent: Most children choose 12, because 12 points is the biggest prize. Do not correct this. The dice will answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of Copy or Crash. Here you guess which chain length scores best.

flow.do: 1. Play the first game to 24 points, with no checker. 2. Keep the score sheet. 3. Ask which length worked best.
flow.say: Play to 24 points. Keep track of which length you chose each turn, and how often each one crashed.
flow.kid: Play to 24 points. Write down the length you chose each turn.

ask.q: Why does the 12-letter chain crash so often?
good: There are 12 chances to roll a 1.
More letters means more chances for a mistake.

flow.parent: With a fair die, a 4-letter copy is perfect about half the time. An 8-letter copy is perfect about one time in four, and a 12-letter copy about one time in nine.
flow.context: This is the first game of Copy or Crash. Here you copy chains with no checker.

flow.do: 1. Play the second game to 24 points, with the checker rule. 2. Compare the number of turns with the first game.
flow.say: Now every 1 gets a second roll. Which chain length is the best choice this time?
flow.kid: Now roll again each time you get a 1. Which length is best now?
flow.parent: With the checker, a 12-letter copy is perfect about seven times in ten. Long chains now win easily.
flow.context: This is the second game of Copy or Crash. Here a checker catches most of the mistakes.

flow.do: 1. Ask what changed between the two games. 2. Explain the puzzle this makes for early RNA.
flow.say: Tell me what changed. Long chains became safe only with a checker. But in a cell, the checker is itself built from a long chain.
flow.kid: What changed in the second game? A good checker needs a long chain. Which came first?
flow.think: A careful copier needs a long chain. A long chain needs a careful copier. How could that have started?

check.q: With a careless copier, which RNA chain is most likely to be copied perfectly?
options: All chains are copied equally well
No chain can ever be copied
check.why: Every letter is one more chance of a mistake, so a short chain is copied perfectly more often. Choosing the long chain mixes up the size of the prize with the chance of winning it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Copy or Crash. Here you say what the two games show about early RNA.

experiments.title: The Salt Water Skin Test: can a soap skin form in sea-salty water?
experiments.question: Soap molecules line up by themselves into thin skins, which we see as foam. Do they make as much foam in water as salty as the sea as they do in plain water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which bottle will have the tallest foam after shaking: plain water, sea-salty water or very salty water? Or will all three be the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three bottles are the same size and hold the same amount of water at the same temperature. Each gets the same amount of the same soap water. The same person shakes each bottle 20 times in the same way. Only one thing changes: how much salt is in the water.

materials.item: clear plastic bottles with caps, all the same size (500 millilitre or 1 litre water bottles)
a plain bath soap bar. Do not use liquid handwash, shampoo or dish liquid for this test
table salt
drinking water at room temperature, and half a tumbler of warm water
a steel tumbler of about 200 millilitres, a teaspoon and a small bowl
a grater or a knife, for the grown-up
a ruler, a marker pen and a notebook

experiments.safety: A grown-up grates the soap. Do not drink the test water. Soap water stings the eyes, so keep the caps on while shaking.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, one for each round. For each bottle write the height of the foam in centimetres. Add one line on what the water looks like: clear, cloudy, or with white specks.
experiments.context: In this experiment you shake the same soap in plain water, in water as salty as the sea, and in very salty water. The foam shows how well the soap molecules can make thin skins. It tests one of the arguments about where the first cells formed.

setup.art: Three identical clear bottles in a row, each one-third full of water and labelled 'plain', 'sea' and 'very salty', with a tumbler and a packet of salt beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bottles: plain water, sea-salty water and very salty water.

setup.art: A small bowl of cloudy soap water with a teaspoon in it, and a hand adding two teaspoons to the first bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Add two teaspoons of soap water to each bottle.

setup.art: A girl shaking a capped bottle up and down with both hands, counting aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Shake each bottle 20 times, the same way.

setup.art: A ruler held against a bottle, measuring the white foam from the water's surface to the top of the foam.
setup.caption: 4. Wait 30 seconds. Measure the foam from the water line to the top.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: height of foam in centimetres

flow.do: 1. Show your child the soap, the salt and the three bottles. 2. Explain that foam is made of thin soap skins. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Foam is thousands of thin soap skins. Which bottle will have the tallest foam: plain, sea-salty or very salty? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three bottles. Guess which will have the tallest foam. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think salt will, or will not, make a difference?
good: Soap does not lather well in the sea.
Salt is just dissolved, so it should not matter.
The salt might get in the way of the soap.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect no difference, because salt and soap seem to have nothing to do with each other.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Salt Water Skin Test. Here you guess which water will make the most foam.

flow.do: 1. Grate about half a teaspoon of soap into the small bowl. 2. Add half a tumbler of warm water. 3. Stir for two minutes until most of the soap has dissolved.
flow.say: This is our soap water. Every bottle will get exactly the same amount of this, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: A grown-up grates the soap. Add warm water and stir for two minutes.
flow.parent: The soap water will look cloudy, and a few bits may be left. That is fine. Stir again each time before you take a spoonful.
flow.context: In this step of the Salt Water Skin Test you make the soap water that goes into all three bottles.

flow.do: 1. Pour one tumbler of drinking water into each bottle. 2. Add no salt to the first, one level teaspoon to the second and four level teaspoons to the third. 3. Cap and shake until the salt has dissolved. 4. Label the bottles.
flow.say: One level teaspoon of salt in a tumbler of water is about as salty as the sea. The third bottle is more than three times as salty as the sea.
flow.kid: Put one tumbler of water in each bottle. Add no salt, one teaspoon, and four teaspoons. Shake until the salt is gone.
flow.parent: Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in every litre. That is 7 grams in a 200 millilitre tumbler, and a level teaspoon of table salt is about 6 grams. If your tap water is hard, such as borewell water, use drinking water or boiled and cooled water for all three bottles.
flow.context: In this step of the Salt Water Skin Test you make plain water, sea-salty water and very salty water.

flow.do: 1. Stir the soap water. Add two teaspoons to each bottle and cap it. 2. Shake each bottle 20 times, the same way. 3. Stand the bottles for 30 seconds. 4. Measure the foam from the water line to the top of the foam, and look at the water.
flow.say: Shake each one 20 times, just as hard each time. Then we wait 30 seconds and measure the foam.
flow.kid: Add two teaspoons of soap water to each bottle. Shake each 20 times. Wait, then measure the foam.

ask.q: What do you notice in the salty bottles, apart from the foam?
good: The water is cloudier.
There are tiny white specks.
The bubbles are bigger and pop sooner.

flow.parent: Count the shakes aloud together. Measure only the foam, not the water. If the foam top is uneven, measure to the middle of the slope.
flow.context: This is round 1 of the Salt Water Skin Test. Here you add soap water, shake and measure the foam.

flow.do: 1. Add two more teaspoons of soap water to each bottle, shake 20 times and measure. That is round 2. 2. Do the same once more for round 3. 3. Write every height in the table.
flow.say: One round can be a fluke. Let's add more soap water and see whether the bottles stay in the same order.
flow.kid: Add two more teaspoons to each bottle. Shake 20 times and measure. Then do it once more.
flow.parent: With a true soap bar, the plain bottle should have clearly the tallest foam in every round. The very salty bottle should have little or none, with cloudy water or white specks. If all three foam alike, your bar is probably a detergent bar. Try a plain washing or bath soap, or add two more teaspoons of salt to the third bottle.
flow.context: These are rounds 2 and 3 of the Salt Water Skin Test. Here you add more soap water and see whether the pattern stays the same.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Have them write the claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 3. Only then read the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Tell me your claim. What did you see that supports it? Why do you think the salt made that difference?
flow.kid: Write your claim. Write what you saw. Write why you think it happened.

ask.q: Where did the soap go in the very salty bottle?
good: It came out of the water as white specks.
The salt pushed it out, so it could not make skins.

ask.q: What does this say about fatty skins forming in the sea?
good: Simple fatty skins may form badly in sea water.
It is a problem for the vent idea, unless a mixture works better.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A soap molecule has a head that mixes with water and a tail that stays away from water. In water the molecules line up into thin skins, and nobody has to arrange them. The particles of dissolved salt push soap molecules out of the water into solid specks. Fewer are left to make skins, so there is less foam. Fatty acids, which may have made the first cell skins, behave like soap. This is a model. A bubble wall is not a cell membrane, but both form because of the same head and tail.

check.q: Soap makes less foam in very salty water. What is the best explanation?
options: Salt pushes soap out of the water
Salty water is too heavy to shake
The salt uses up all the air
check.why: Dissolved salt makes soap molecules clump into solid specks, so fewer are free to line up into skins. Choosing 'kills' treats soap as alive. Choosing 'too heavy' or 'air' misses that the same shaking and the same air were used in every bottle.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Salt Water Skin Test. Here you say what you found and what it means for the first cell skins.

experiments.title: Hot Vent in a Jar: where does hot water go in cold water?
experiments.question: A small bottle of hot coloured water is lowered into a jar of cold water. Does the hot water stay in the bottle, sink, spread sideways or rise? Does cold coloured water do the same?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will the hot coloured water do when the bottle reaches the bottom? What will the cold coloured water do? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both small bottles are the same size, filled to the brim, with the same amount of colour. Both are lowered gently into the same jar of fresh cold water. Only one thing changes: the water in one small bottle is hot and in the other it is cold.
results_table: What the colour did in the first 10 seconds
Seconds for the colour to reach the top
Where the colour was after 2 minutes

materials.item: a large clear container at least 15 centimetres deep (a big glass jar, a clear plastic dabba or a clear jug)
small glass bottles with narrow mouths (empty ink, medicine or food-colour bottles)
string, about 40 centimetres for each small bottle
food colour or ink. Strong black tea or coffee also works
hot water from a kettle, for the grown-up, and cold tap water
a watch or phone timer, and a notebook

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and lowers the hot bottle. Use water that is hot but not boiling, so the small bottle does not crack.
experiments.record: Draw the jar twice, once for the hot bottle and once for the cold bottle. Show with coloured pencil where the colour went. Write the time the colour took to reach the top.
experiments.context: In this experiment you lower a small bottle of hot coloured water into cold water and watch where it goes. Then you repeat with cold coloured water. It shows why water comes up out of a vent.

setup.caption: 1. Fill the big jar with cold water. Let the water become still.

setup.caption: 2. A grown-up fills a small bottle with hot coloured water and lowers it to the bottom.
