A coloured layer at the top
The colour stayed in the bottle
It did not reach the top
Still in the bottle, a little spilled at the bottom

flow.do: 1. Fill the big jar with cold tap water and leave it to become still. 2. Tie a string round the neck of each small bottle. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write them down.
flow.say: One small bottle will hold hot red water and one cold red water. What will each do at the bottom of this jar? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill the big jar with cold water. Guess where the hot colour will go. Say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children expect the colour to spread out evenly in all directions.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hot Vent in a Jar. Here you set up and guess where hot water will go.

flow.do: 1. Put three drops of colour in a small bottle and fill it to the brim with hot water. 2. Hold the string and lower the bottle slowly, upright, to the bottom. 3. Your child starts the timer and watches from the side.
flow.say: Watch the mouth of the bottle. Tell me what the colour does, and call out when it reaches the top.
flow.kid: Watch from the side. Where does the colour go? Time how long it takes to reach the top.
flow.parent: Lower the bottle slowly so the water in the jar stays still. A thin coloured stream should rise from the mouth within seconds and spread under the surface.
flow.context: In this step of Hot Vent in a Jar a grown-up lowers the hot coloured bottle and you watch.

flow.do: 1. Empty the big jar and refill it with fresh cold water. Let it settle. 2. Fill the second small bottle with cold coloured water. 3. Lower it in the same way and watch for two minutes.
flow.say: Now the same test with cold coloured water. Watch the mouth of the bottle again.
flow.kid: Now lower the cold coloured bottle. Watch for two minutes. What is different?
flow.parent: The cold colour should mostly stay in the bottle. A little may spill out and lie on the bottom. This second bottle shows that it is the heat, not the colour, that makes the water rise.
flow.context: In this step of Hot Vent in a Jar you repeat the test with cold coloured water.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. 2. Have them draw both jars. 3. Then explain, using the note below.
flow.say: What is your claim? What did you see? Why do you think hot water went up and cold water did not?
flow.kid: Say your claim. Say what you saw. Draw both jars with the colour.

ask.q: At a real vent, what would the rising hot water carry up with it?
good: Minerals dissolved from the rock.
Gases such as hydrogen.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. When water is heated, its molecules move faster and take up a little more room. So a cup of hot water weighs slightly less than a cup of cold water. The lighter hot water is pushed up by the heavier cold water around it. At a vent, water heated in the rock rises the same way. It carries dissolved minerals up, and they turn solid in the cold sea and build the chimney.

check.q: Why does hot water rise through cold water?
options: Hot water is lighter for its size
The colour pulls the water up
Cold water sucks the hot water up
check.why: Heated water spreads out a little, so the same amount takes more room and is lighter for its size. The heavier cold water pushes it up. Choosing 'heat always travels upwards' mixes up heat with hot water. Heat can travel in any direction.

flow.context: This is the last step of Hot Vent in a Jar. Here you explain why hot water rises, and what that means at a vent.

activities.title: Deep Time on Your Arms: work out your own scale
activities.context: In this activity a string as long as your arm span stands for the whole age of the Earth. You work out how many million years one centimetre stands for. Then you mark when life began, and when people arrived.

materials.item: string or wool, a little longer than your arm span
a measuring tape or a ruler
clothes clips
small paper labels and sticky tape, or sticky notes
a pencil and a notebook. A calculator is allowed

activities.record: Write your arm span, your scale in million years for each centimetre, and the distance of each event from the Today end.

setup.art: A girl with arms stretched wide while her mother holds a string from one middle fingertip to the other.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a string as long as your arm span.

setup.art: The string laid straight on the floor beside a measuring tape, with four clothes clips clipped along it.
setup.caption: 2. Clip on your guesses. Then measure the string and work out the scale.

setup.art: The same string with paper labels taped along it, most of them crowded near one end.
setup.caption: 3. Divide to find each event's place. Tape on the labels.

flow.do: 1. Cut a string as long as your child's arm span, fingertip to fingertip. 2. Lay it straight on the floor. One end is the day the Earth formed, and the other end is today. 3. Your child clips on four guesses.
flow.say: This string is the whole age of the Earth. Clip where you think each of these belongs: the first cells, the first animals you could see, the end of the dinosaurs, the first people.
flow.kid: The string is all of Earth's time. Clip on four guesses: first cells, first animals, last dinosaurs, first people.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Most people put animals and dinosaurs near the middle, and people several centimetres from the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of Deep Time on Your Arms. Here you guess where four events belong.

flow.do: 1. Measure the string in centimetres. Round it to the nearest 5. 2. The Earth is about 4,500 million years old. Divide 4,500 by the length of the string. 3. Write the answer, rounded to a whole number. This is the scale.
flow.say: Every centimetre must stand for the same number of years. How many million years is one centimetre of your string? Divide 4,500 by its length.
flow.kid: Measure the string. Divide 4,500 by its length. That is your scale.
flow.parent: For a string of 125 centimetres, 4,500 divided by 125 is 36. So 1 centimetre stands for 36 million years. For 130 centimetres the scale is about 35, and for 140 centimetres about 32.
flow.context: In this step of Deep Time on Your Arms you work out how many million years one centimetre stands for.

flow.do: 1. Read the table of events. 2. For each event, divide the number of million years ago by the scale. That is the distance in centimetres from the Today end. 3. Measure, and tape on a label.
flow.say: To find an event's place, divide how long ago it was by your scale. Measure that far from the Today end and tape on the label.
flow.kid: Divide each age by your scale. Measure from the Today end. Tape on the label.

chart.title: Events to mark, with an example for a string of 125 cm (1 cm stands for 36 million years)
cols: Example: cm from the Today end
rows: LUCA, the ancestor of all cells today (an estimate)
Oldest fossils that almost all scientists accept
Oxygen begins to build up in the air
First animals big enough to see
less than a tenth of a millimetre
chart.note: The dates come from rocks and fossils and are rounded. The date for LUCA is an estimate from one study in 2024.

flow.parent: The last label cannot be placed with a ruler. Tape it over the very end of the string. Human beings like us take up less than the thickness of a hair.
flow.context: In this step of Deep Time on Your Arms you divide to find each event's place on the string.

flow.do: 1. Compare the labels with the four clips. 2. Your child holds the string across their arms. 3. Ask what surprised them.
flow.say: Hold the string across your arms. Where is the start of life? Where are the animals? What surprised you most?
flow.kid: Hold the string across your arms. Compare your guesses with the labels. What surprised you?
flow.think: For most of the string, every living being was a single cell. Why do you think big bodies took so long?

check.q: On your arm span model, where do the first animals big enough to see belong?
options: About a hand's length from the Today fingertip
Right in the middle of your chest
check.why: Animals big enough to see appeared about 570 million years ago, which is about one eighth of Earth's history. Choosing the middle of the chest is the commonest guess. It shows how short the time of animals feels until you measure it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Deep Time on Your Arms. Here you compare your guesses with the measured places.

activities.title: Acid Sea, Alkaline Vent: the turmeric test
activities.context: In this activity you use turmeric paper to tell alkaline liquids from acid ones. Then you let an alkaline liquid and an acid liquid meet on one strip. This is the kind of difference the alkaline vent idea depends on.

materials.item: turmeric powder
white paper, a tissue or a paper napkin, cut into 6 strips
baking soda (cooking soda)
a lemon, or a spoon of vinegar or tamarind water
a little soap water and plain water
small bowls or steel katoris, and spoons
an old plate and old newspaper. Turmeric stains

activities.safety: Turmeric stains clothes and tables. Work on old newspaper and wear old clothes.
activities.record: Draw each strip and colour it as you saw it. Under each write 'acid', 'alkaline' or 'neither'.

setup.art: A child painting bright yellow turmeric water onto strips of white paper laid on newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Paint paper strips with turmeric water.

setup.art: Four yellow strips in a row, each with a drop of a different liquid, one drop turning the paper red-brown.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of each liquid on its own strip.

setup.art: One yellow strip with a red-brown patch spreading from the left end and a pale yellow wet patch spreading from the right end, meeting at a clear line in the middle.
setup.caption: 3. On a fresh strip, let baking soda water and lemon juice meet.

flow.do: 1. Stir half a teaspoon of turmeric into two spoons of water. 2. Paint the yellow water onto 6 paper strips. 3. Stir a teaspoon of baking soda into a quarter tumbler of water. Squeeze the lemon into another bowl.
flow.say: Turmeric changes colour in alkaline liquids. Which of our four liquids do you think will change it: lemon juice, baking soda water, soap water or plain water? Why?
flow.kid: Paint six strips yellow with turmeric water. Guess which liquids will change the colour.
flow.parent: The strips work while still damp. Write the guess down before any liquid touches the paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Acid Sea, Alkaline Vent. Here you make turmeric paper and guess which liquids will change its colour.

flow.do: 1. Put one drop of each liquid on its own strip. 2. Watch for one minute. 3. Sort the strips into 'turned red' and 'stayed yellow'.
flow.say: Watch each strip. Tell me which ones change. What do the liquids that turn it red have in common?
flow.kid: Put one drop on each strip. Which strips turn red? Which stay yellow?

ask.q: What do baking soda water and soap water have in common?
good: Both feel slippery.
Both are alkaline.
Neither is sour.

flow.parent: Baking soda water and soap water turn the paper red-brown, because they are alkaline. Lemon juice and plain water leave it yellow. Turmeric shows alkaline liquids only. It does not tell acid from plain water.
flow.context: In this step of Acid Sea, Alkaline Vent you test four liquids on turmeric paper.

flow.do: 1. Take a fresh strip. Put three drops of baking soda water at one end. Put three drops of lemon juice at the other end. 2. Watch the two wet patches spread until they meet. 3. Then drip lemon juice onto a red patch.
flow.say: Watch the place where the two meet. What do you see there? Now drip lemon juice on the red. What happens?
flow.kid: Put baking soda water at one end and lemon juice at the other. Watch where they meet.

ask.q: Why does the red turn yellow again under lemon juice?
good: The acid cancels the alkaline liquid.
Acid and alkaline are opposites.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. A red patch ends in a clear line where the acid begins. Inside an alkaline vent chimney, alkaline vent water and the slightly acid early sea were kept apart like this, by thin mineral walls. Every living cell today makes energy from such a difference across the cell membrane. The paper shows the difference. It does not show energy being made.

check.q: In the alkaline vent idea, what gave the first chemistry of life its energy?
options: The difference between vent water and sea water
check.why: The idea says energy came from alkaline water and acid sea water meeting across a thin wall. Sunlight does not reach the deep sea floor, so choosing sunlight mixes vents up with plants.

flow.context: This is the last step of Acid Sea, Alkaline Vent. Here an alkaline liquid and an acid liquid meet on one strip.

activities.title: Find the Ancestor: what did LUCA have?
activities.context: In this activity you compare four living beings of very different kinds. From what they share, you work out what their shared ancestor must have had. This is how scientists describe LUCA, the ancestor of all cells.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
two colour pencils

activities.record: Copy the table. Circle in one colour every feature that all four share. Write two lists: 'LUCA probably had' and 'came later'.

setup.art: A notebook page with a hand-drawn table of four columns headed with small drawings of a bacterium, an archaeon, a yeast cell and a girl.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the table of four living beings.

setup.art: The same table with some rows circled in green and others in orange.
setup.caption: 2. Circle what all four share in one colour.

setup.art: A simple tree drawn below the table, four tips joining down to one cell at the base with a list beside it.
setup.caption: 3. List what the shared ancestor must have had.

flow.do: 1. Ask how we could know what a great-great-grandmother was like if no photograph exists. 2. Listen to the ideas. 3. Explain that biologists use the same reasoning for the ancestor of all cells.
flow.say: Suppose you and all your cousins have the same shape of ear lobe. What would you guess about your shared grandmother's ears? Why?
flow.kid: You and all your cousins share a feature. What can you guess about your grandmother? Why?

ask.q: Is it certain that she had it?
good: No, but it is the simplest explanation.
It is likely, not certain.

flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Ancestor. Here you think about how to learn about an ancestor nobody has seen.

flow.do: 1. Your child copies the table. 2. They circle every row where all four say yes. 3. They write those features under 'LUCA probably had', and the rest under 'came later'.
flow.say: Circle each feature that all four have. If all four have a feature, where did they most likely get it from?
flow.kid: Copy the table. Circle every feature that all four share. List them.

chart.title: Four living beings from very different branches of life
rows: DNA as the store of instructions
ATP made by a flow of protons

flow.parent: The first six rows are shared by all four. So the shared ancestor most likely had all six already. The last four rows are not shared by all, so they most likely came later on some branches.
flow.context: In this step of Find the Ancestor you compare four living beings and find what all of them share.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether LUCA needed oxygen, and how your child knows. 2. Ask whether LUCA was the first living being. 3. Explain what the 2016 and 2024 studies added.
flow.say: Did LUCA need oxygen? How can you tell from the table? And was LUCA the very first life?
flow.kid: Did LUCA need oxygen? Use the table. Was LUCA the very first life?

ask.q: LUCA already had ribosomes and a code. What does that tell you?
good: A lot had happened before LUCA.
LUCA was not the first life.

flow.parent: Three of the four live without oxygen, so the ancestor most likely did too. Rocks agree: the air held almost no oxygen until about 2,400 million years ago. LUCA was already a full cell, so simpler life must have come before. Real studies compare thousands of genes from thousands of species in this way.

check.q: Bacteria, archaea, yeast and humans all have ribosomes. What is the simplest explanation?
options: Ribosomes spread between them like a cold
check.why: One ancestor passing a feature down is far simpler than four separate inventions of the same complicated machine. Choosing 'each invented' would need the same unlikely thing to happen four times.

flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Ancestor. Here you use the table to say what LUCA was like.

activities.title: Drying Drops: what happens to dissolved things when water dries?
activities.context: In this activity you let drops of salty turmeric water dry on a steel plate. You see where the salt and the colour end up. It shows why pools that dry out could help small molecules to join.

materials.item: a steel plate
salt and turmeric powder
water
a spoon
a sunny window sill or balcony

schedule.what: Mix the salty turmeric water, guess, and put five drops on the plate in the sun.
Look at the dried drops, draw one, and explain where the salt and colour went.

activities.record: Draw one drop when wet and the same drop when dry. Mark where the colour and the salt are.

setup.art: A spoon letting drops of pale yellow water fall onto a steel plate on a sunny window sill.
setup.caption: 1. Put five drops of salty turmeric water on a steel plate.

setup.art: The same plate later, each drop now a dry ring with a darker yellow edge and tiny white crystals.
setup.caption: 2. When the drops are dry, look closely at the edges.

flow.do: 1. Stir a pinch of salt and a pinch of turmeric into half a tumbler of water. 2. Ask where the salt and the colour will be when a drop has dried, and why. 3. Put five separate drops on the steel plate and leave it in the sun.
flow.say: The salt is spread all through this water. When a drop dries, where will the salt and the yellow be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mix salt and turmeric in water. Guess where they go when a drop dries. Put five drops on the plate.
flow.wait: Leave the plate until the drops are fully dry. In strong sun this takes an hour or two. Indoors, leave it overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drying Drops. Here you guess what drying will do, and set the drops out.

flow.do: 1. Look at the dry drops, with a magnifying glass if you have one. 2. Your child draws one. 3. Ask what they saw first, then explain.
flow.say: Look at the edge of each dried drop. What do you see? How far apart were the salt particles before, and how far apart now?
flow.kid: Look closely at the dry drops. Draw one. Where are the salt and the colour now?

ask.q: Why might crowding help small molecules to join into chains?
good: They can only join if they touch.
In lots of water they rarely meet.

flow.parent: The salt and colour usually end up packed in a ring at the edge, with tiny square salt crystals. After your child has described this, explain. As water leaves, everything dissolved is crowded into less and less space. In a pool that dries, building blocks are pushed against each other and can join. With the water gone, the joins are also less likely to be broken again.

check.q: A pool of water with building blocks in it dries up. What happens to the building blocks?
check.why: Only the water leaves, so the dissolved things are packed into less space. Choosing 'they leave with the water' is a common idea. The white ring of salt on your plate shows that they stay.

flow.context: This is the last step of Drying Drops. Here you look at the dried drops and explain what drying did.

projects.title: The Origin Case File: vents or pools?
projects.context: In this three-day project you build a case file, as a detective would, on where life began. You use your own test results and the findings of scientists. You finish with your verdict and say what evidence would change your mind.

materials.item: a large sheet of chart paper, or four notebook pages
sketch pens or colour pencils
your results from the Salt Water Skin Test and any other tests you did
the evidence cards from the game Vent, Pool or Both, if you made them

schedule.what: Draw the two suspects: an alkaline vent and a warm pool. Label what each offers a first cell: skin, instructions and energy.
Sort the evidence for and against each. Add your own test results as evidence, with your numbers.
Write the verdict, what is still unknown, and one new test you would do. Present the file in three minutes.

projects.record: One chart with two columns, vents and pools. Each column has a drawing, a list of evidence for, a list of evidence against, and your own results. Below both: your verdict and what would change your mind.

setup.art: A chart paper divided down the middle, with white chimneys drawn on the left half and a steaming pool on the right half.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the two places and label what each offers.

setup.art: A girl taping small evidence cards under the two drawings, some with a green tick and some with a red cross.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the evidence for and against each place.

setup.art: The girl standing beside the finished chart, pointing at a box at the bottom labelled 'My verdict'.
setup.caption: 3. Give your verdict and say what would change your mind.

flow.do: 1. Your child divides the chart in two and draws an alkaline vent and a warm pool. 2. Under each, they write how it could give a first cell a skin, instructions and energy. 3. Where a place gives no clear answer, they write a question mark.
flow.say: A first cell needed a skin, instructions and energy. Draw each place. Then write how it could supply each of the three.
flow.kid: Draw a vent and a pool. For each, write how it gives skin, instructions and energy.
flow.parent: A strong chart has question marks. The vent has no clear way to join RNA chains under water. The pool has no steady energy supply like the vent's.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Origin Case File. Here you draw the two places and what each offers.

flow.do: 1. Your child lists the evidence for and against each place. 2. They add their own foam heights from the Salt Water Skin Test. 3. They mark each item as strong or weak evidence.
flow.say: Now the evidence. What did your own salt test show, and which side does it help? Is it strong evidence or weak?
flow.kid: List evidence for and against each place. Add your own test results. Mark each strong or weak.

ask.q: Your soap test used table salt and bath soap. Why is that weaker evidence than a laboratory test?
good: Soap foam is only a model of a cell skin.
The sea has other salts too.
Early fatty molecules were a mixture.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the Origin Case File. Here you sort the evidence and add your own results.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a verdict: vents, pools, both or not enough evidence. 2. They write one finding that would change their mind. 3. They present the file to the family in three minutes.
flow.say: Give your verdict and your best reason. Then tell us what finding would make you change your mind.
flow.kid: Write your verdict and your best reason. Say what would change your mind. Present your file.
flow.parent: 'Not enough evidence yet' is a fully acceptable verdict, if your child can say what is missing. Scientists themselves have not agreed.
flow.think: Is it harder to say 'I don't know yet' than to pick a side? Why?
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Origin Case File. Here you give your verdict and present the file.

challenges.title: Foam in the Sea: make a skin that lasts in salty water
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Salt Water Skin Test, bath soap made little foam in sea-salty water. Here you try to make a mix that foams well in that same salty water. Scientists faced the same problem with the first cell skins.
challenges.problem: Make a mix that gives at least 3 centimetres of foam in sea-salty water after 20 shakes. The foam must still be there after one minute.
constraints: Use the same bottle and the same sea-salty water as in the Salt Water Skin Test: one level teaspoon of salt in one tumbler of water.
Add no more than four teaspoons of your mix in total.
Change only one thing at a time, and write down each try.
Shake 20 times, wait one minute, then measure.
materials: the bottles, salt, tumbler, teaspoon and ruler from the Salt Water Skin Test
bath soap water left from the test
other things that clean: dish liquid, shampoo, washing powder, a soap made with coconut oil, soapnut (reetha) or shikakai if you have them
general: Add more of the same soap water, up to the limit of four teaspoons.
Use warm sea-salty water, because more soap stays dissolved in warm water.
Swap the bath soap for dish liquid or shampoo. These are detergents, made to work in salty and hard water.
creative: Mix two different cleaners, such as one teaspoon of soap water and one of shampoo. A mixture sometimes works where each one alone does not.
Soak two soapnut shells in warm water for ten minutes and try the brown water. Soapnut foam comes from a different kind of molecule made by the tree.
Try a soap made mostly from coconut oil. Sailors once used such soaps for washing in sea water.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own mix. Write the recipe, test it and measure the foam at 30 seconds and at one minute. Did a mixture beat each of its parts? In 2019, scientists found that a mixture of 12 fatty molecules made skins in salty water where single ones had failed.

setup.art: A bottle of sea-salty water beside small bowls of soap water, dish liquid, shampoo and brown soapnut water, each with a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 1. Collect things that might foam in salty water.

setup.art: A girl shaking a bottle while her younger brother watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Add your mix, shake 20 times and wait one minute.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of recipes and foam heights, one row circled.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the foam and write down each try.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of the foam heights from the Salt Water Skin Test. 2. Make a fresh bottle of sea-salty water. 3. Ask what might help a skin to form in salty water.
flow.say: Bath soap made little foam in sea-salty water. What could we change so that a skin forms anyway? Why might that work?
flow.kid: Bath soap made little foam in salty water. What could you change? Why might it work?
flow.context: This is the first step of Foam in the Sea. Here you think of ways to make foam in sea-salty water.

flow.do: 1. Try one of the usual solutions. 2. Shake 20 times, wait one minute and measure. 3. Rinse the bottle and refill it with fresh sea-salty water before the next try.
flow.say: Change one thing only. Shake, wait a minute and measure. Write the recipe and the height.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Shake 20 times and wait one minute. Measure and write it down.
flow.parent: Dish liquid and shampoo usually pass easily. That is the point. Chemists designed their molecules so that salt does not push them out of the water.
flow.context: In this step of Foam in the Sea you test one usual solution at a time.

flow.do: 1. Try a mixture of two cleaners, or soapnut water. 2. Test each part alone as well, with the same total amount. 3. Compare the three heights.
flow.say: Now a mixture. To know whether mixing helped, we must also test each part alone.
flow.kid: Try a mixture. Test each part alone too. Which gives the most foam?

ask.q: Why must each part also be tested alone?
good: Otherwise we cannot tell whether mixing helped.
One part may be doing all the work.

flow.context: In this step of Foam in the Sea you test whether a mixture beats its parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes their best recipe and its foam height. 2. Ask what the result suggests about the first cell skins. 3. Read the last lines of the challenge together.
flow.say: Which recipe won? The first fatty skins were not bath soap. What might the early sea have had that our first test left out?
flow.kid: Write your best recipe. What might the early sea have had that plain soap lacks?
flow.think: Our first test said skins fail in salty water. A different mix said they can form. What does that teach you about trusting one test?
flow.context: This is the last step of Foam in the Sea. Here you choose your best recipe and say what it suggests.

items.p: Which three things do scientists look for together in a first cell?
opts: A skin, copied instructions and an energy supply
A nucleus, a brain and blood
items.why: A cell needs a membrane, instructions that can be copied, and steady energy. Choosing sunlight, soil and air lists what a plant needs today, not what a first cell needed.

items.p: An opening in the sea floor where hot water comes out is called a hydrothermal ____.
items.why: Sea water seeps into the rock, is heated, and rises out again through a vent.

items.p: True or false: plants are the food makers at deep-sea vents.
items.why: False. No sunlight reaches the deep sea floor. Bacteria and archaea make the food there, using energy from chemicals. This is called chemosynthesis.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.why: These are the main words of the unit. A strong answer can also give an example of each.
pairs: Ribozyme
RNA that works as a catalyst
Membrane
the thin skin round a cell
LUCA
the ancestor of all cells alive today
Hypothesis
an idea that can be tested
Chemosynthesis
making food with energy from chemicals

items.p: Sort each feature: black smoker or alkaline vent?
items.why: Black smokers sit over melted rock and are very hot, acid and dark. Alkaline vents are warmed by rock reacting with sea water, and are warm, alkaline and white.
items: Heated by rock reacting with sea water

items.p: Why does RNA solve the puzzle of 'which came first, instructions or workers'?
opts: RNA is found only in humans
items.why: RNA carries instructions in its letters and can also act as a catalyst. Choosing 'strongest' is the opposite of the truth: RNA is fragile, which is one problem for the idea.

items.p: The same soap made tall foam in plain water and little foam in very salty water. Explain why.
items.a: Soap molecules line up into thin skins in water, and foam is made of those skins. Dissolved salt pushes soap molecules out of the water into solid specks. Fewer are left to make skins, so there is less foam.
items.why: A strong answer says what foam is made of, and what the salt does to the soap molecules.

items.p: Put these events in order, from longest ago to most recent.
a: LUCA, the ancestor of all cells today, lives
Oxygen builds up in the air
The first animals big enough to see
items.why: The Earth formed about 4,500 million years ago and LUCA lived perhaps 4,200 million years ago. Oxygen built up from 2,400, animals appeared about 570, the big dinosaurs died out 66, and humans like us are 0.3 million years old.
items: Oxygen builds up in the air
LUCA, the ancestor of all cells today, lives
The first animals big enough to see

items.p: A string of 150 centimetres stands for 4,500 million years. What does 1 centimetre stand for?
items.why: 4,500 ÷ 150 = 30. So each centimetre stands for 30 million years. Choosing 150 mixes up the length of the string with the scale.

items.p: True or false: LUCA was the very first living being.
items.why: False. LUCA already had a membrane, DNA, ribosomes and the genetic code. Simpler life must have come before LUCA.

items.p: Draw an alkaline vent chimney cut open. Show the vent water, the sea water and the thin walls between.
items.a: A white chimney with many small chambers. Warm alkaline water rises inside. Cold, slightly acid sea water is outside. Thin mineral walls separate the two.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two different waters kept apart by a thin wall. That difference is the energy source in the alkaline vent idea.
items.art: A blank outline of a tall chimney on the sea floor.

items.p: Three of these support the pool idea. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Drying joins building blocks into chains
Fatty skins form well in fresh water
Ultraviolet light helps make RNA building blocks
All cells use a flow of protons
items.why: The flow of protons across a membrane fits the vent idea, because a vent chimney has such a difference naturally. The other three fit pools on land.

items.p: The huge stretch of time in Earth's history, counted in millions and billions of years, is called ____ time.
items.why: The words 'deep time' were first used by the writer John McPhee in 1981.

items.p: Two children argue about where life began.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, or says there is not enough evidence, and gives at least one finding. It also says what the other child has right.
items.why: Scientists themselves disagree. Kavya has the steady energy and the proton evidence. Nila has the drying and the fresh water skins. Both are using real evidence.

views.says: Life began at deep-sea vents, because they give steady energy for thousands of years.
Life began in pools on land, because drying joins building blocks into chains.

items.ask: Whom do you agree with more? Give one piece of evidence. Then say one thing the other child has right.

items.p: Hot coloured water rose from a small bottle through cold water. What does this explain about a vent?
items.a: Heated water is lighter for its size than cold water, so it is pushed upwards. Water heated inside the sea floor rises out of the vent the same way, carrying dissolved minerals with it.
items.why: A strong answer links the test to the vent: heating makes water lighter, so it rises and carries minerals up.

items.p: What is the best evidence inside your own cells for an RNA world?
opts: The ribosome's working part is RNA
Cells contain a lot of water
DNA is kept in the nucleus
Cells are too small to see
items.why: The machine that builds every protein has RNA at its working centre. That looks like a leftover from a time when RNA did the work. The other facts are true but say nothing about RNA coming first.

items.p: True or false: scientists have made an RNA that copies all of itself, again and again, with no help.
items.why: False, as far as we know. Ribozymes that copy other short RNA chains have been made, and they keep improving. Full self-copying is still a missing step.

items.p: A molecule that speeds up a chemical change without being used up is a ____.
items.why: Enzymes are catalysts made of protein. Ribozymes are catalysts made of RNA.

items.p: A die is rolled once for each letter. A 1 is a mistake. Which chain is copied perfectly most often?
items.why: Each letter is one more chance to roll a 1. Four rolls avoid a 1 about half the time. Twelve rolls avoid it about one time in nine.

items.p: A careful copier needs a long RNA chain. A long chain needs a careful copier. Why is this a puzzle?
items.a: Each one seems to need the other to exist first. A long chain cannot survive careless copying, so the careful copier could not be kept. But without a long chain there is no careful copier.
items.why: This is called Eigen's paradox. A strong answer shows that neither could come first alone, and may suggest a way out, such as short chains working together.

items.p: Match each thing to what it may have given the first cells.
items.why: A first cell needed a skin, instructions and energy, and the building blocks for all three. Each of these could have supplied one part.
pairs: Fatty acids
a skin that forms by itself
RNA
instructions and a catalyst in one molecule
An alkaline vent
steady energy from a difference across a wall
A pool that dries out
building blocks joined into chains
Meteorites
some ready-made building blocks

items.p: Sort each finding: does it support vents, or pools?
items.why: Vents offer steady energy, shelter and a natural proton difference. Pools offer drying, fresh water and sunlight.
items: All cells make ATP with a flow of protons
The deep sea is sheltered from ultraviolet light
Fatty acid bubbles form in spring water, not sea water
LUCA's oldest genes fit a hydrogen-eating microbe
RNA chains break apart in water

items.p: Four very different living beings all have ribosomes. What does that suggest?
opts: They all live in the same place
They all eat the same food
items.why: A complicated feature shared by all branches was most likely inherited from one ancestor. Inventing the same machine four separate times is far less likely.

items.p: Label a drawing of a protocell: fatty skin, water inside, RNA chain, water outside.
items.why: A protocell is a bubble with a skin of fatty molecules and other molecules, such as RNA, inside. It is a laboratory model, not a living cell.
items.art: A simple round bubble with a double-line skin and a short wavy chain inside, with four blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: most animals at vents today use no oxygen from the sunlit sea.
items.why: False. Most vent animals, and many vent microbes, use oxygen dissolved in sea water. That oxygen was made by photosynthesis. Only some microbes there live with no oxygen at all.

items.p: On a 125 centimetre arm span, 1 centimetre is 36 million years. Where is 570 million years ago?
opts: About 16 cm from the Today end
About 57 cm from the Today end
About 36 cm from the Today end
items.why: 570 ÷ 36 is about 16. So the first animals big enough to see sit about a hand's length from the fingertip.

items.p: Soap foam is only a model of a cell skin. Name one way it is like one and one way it differs.
items.a: Alike: both are thin skins that form by themselves, because the molecules have a head that mixes with water and a tail that does not. Different: a bubble wall is a film of water in air, and a cell membrane is a double layer of fatty molecules in water.
items.why: Knowing where a model stops being true is part of using it honestly.

items.p: Three of these were probably in LUCA. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Bacteria and archaea have no nucleus, so the nucleus most likely appeared later, on one branch. The other three are shared by all cells.

items.p: Two scientists argue about which came first.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For RNA first: ribozymes and the ribosome. For reactions first: RNA is fragile and hard to make, and vents supply energy for simple reactions.
items.why: Both views are held by working scientists. Each explains something the other finds hard.

views.says: Copied instructions came first, as RNA. Without copying, nothing can improve over generations.
Simple reactions fed by vent energy came first. RNA is too hard to make at the very start.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give one reason. What would the other scientist say back?

items.p: Draw fatty acid molecules in water forming a skin. Show which way the heads and tails point.
items.a: Two rows of tadpole-shaped molecules. The round heads face the water on both sides. The tails point inwards, towards each other, away from the water.
items.why: The skin forms because tails stay away from water and heads mix with it. Nobody has to arrange the molecules.
items.art: A blank box labelled 'water' with one tadpole-shaped molecule drawn as an example.

items.p: A book says: 'Scientists know that life began at deep-sea vents.' What is wrong with this sentence?
items.a: Scientists do not know where life began. Vents are one leading idea, with real evidence for and against. Warm pools on land are another. The sentence should say 'some scientists think'.
items.why: A strong answer separates what is known from what is a hypothesis, and names the other idea.

items.p: One arm span stands for 4,500 million years. The universe is 13,800 million years old. How many arm spans?
items.why: 13,800 ÷ 4,500 is a little more than 3. So the Earth has existed for about one third of the age of the universe.

items.p: Foam was 6 cm in plain water and 2 cm in sea-salty water. How do the two compare?
opts: Plain water gave 3 times as much
Plain water gave 4 times as much
Sea-salty water gave 3 times as much
items.why: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. The plain bottle had three times as much foam. Subtracting gives the difference, 4 centimetres, which is not 'times as much'.

items.p: True or false: if one test shows skins fail in salty water, the vent idea is proved wrong.
items.why: False. One test with one kind of molecule cannot settle it. A later test with a mixture of 12 fatty molecules did form skins in warm, salty, alkaline water.

items.p: Put these steps of a possible path to a first cell in a sensible order.
a: Small building blocks form from simple chemicals
Building blocks join into chains such as RNA
Some chains begin to copy other chains
Chains are wrapped inside fatty skins
Protocells grow, split and pass on their chains
items.why: This is one sensible order, and scientists argue about it. Some think the skins or the energy reactions came before copying.
items: Chains are wrapped inside fatty skins
Small building blocks form from simple chemicals
Protocells grow, split and pass on their chains
Some chains begin to copy other chains
Building blocks join into chains such as RNA

items.p: Why can we not simply look for the first cell as a fossil?
items.a: The first cells were tiny and soft, with no hard parts. They lived about 4 billion years ago, and almost no rock that old is left on Earth. The few rocks that remain have been heated and squeezed.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: what the first cells were like, and what has happened to the oldest rocks.

items.p: The reaction of sea water with green olivine rock, which warms alkaline vents, is called ____.
items.why: The reaction makes a rock called serpentine. It gives out heat, makes hydrogen gas and makes the water alkaline.

items.p: Why is hydrogen in the jets of Saturn's moon Enceladus exciting?
opts: It hints at vents on that sea floor
Hydrogen means the moon is burning
It shows the ocean is fresh water
items.why: On Earth, rock reacting with sea water at alkaline vents makes hydrogen. So hydrogen suggests similar vents there. It is not evidence of life itself.

items.p: Match each old belief to the finding that changed it.
items.why: Each belief seemed reasonable until someone found evidence against it. That is how the story of life's origin keeps changing.
pairs: All sea-floor life depends on sunlight
crowds of animals at vents in 1977
Only proteins can be catalysts
an RNA that cut itself in 1982
Every vent needs a volcano
white towers on cold rock in 2000
Building blocks of life need living beings
amino acids from gases and sparks in 1952

items.p: Sort each statement: known, or still an idea?
items.why: The first three have strong evidence that almost all scientists accept. The last three are hypotheses that are still being tested.
items: All cells today share one ancestor
RNA can act as a catalyst
Fatty molecules form skins by themselves
RNA came before DNA and proteins

items.p: Two children argue about looking for life on Enceladus, an ocean moon with no land.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the answer depends on where life began on Earth. If life needs drying pools, an ocean moon is a poor place. If life began at vents, the moon is a good place. So finding or not finding life there would be evidence about our own beginning.
items.why: This shows how a question about another world tests an idea about this one.

views.says: It is a good place to look. It has water, vents and hydrogen.
It is a poor place. With no land there are no pools to dry out.

items.ask: Which idea about life's beginning does each child's view depend on? What would finding life there tell us?

items.p: Draw Earth's history on a clock face of 12 hours. Mark the first animals and the first humans.
items.a: Twelve hours stand for 4,500 million years, so one hour is 375 million years. The first animals big enough to see, 570 million years ago, come about one and a half hours before the end, near half past ten. Humans like us come in about the last 3 seconds.
items.why: 570 ÷ 375 is about 1.5 hours. For humans, 0.3 ÷ 4,500 of 12 hours is about 3 seconds.
items.art: A blank clock face with only the 12 marked.

items.p: True or false: a few copying mistakes are needed for new kinds of RNA chain to appear.
items.why: True. With no mistakes, every copy is the same as its parent, so nothing new can appear. Too many mistakes lose the message. A small number allows change.

items.p: Three of these are problems for the pool idea. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Little dry land on the young Earth
items.why: Water breaking chains is a problem for vents, which never dry. The other three are problems for pools on land.

items.p: Think of one test you could do at home or in a laboratory to learn more about how life began. Describe it.
items.a: Answers will differ. A strong answer names what is changed, what is measured and what is kept the same. An example is testing whether soap skins form better in warm or cold salty water.
items.why: Designing a fair test is harder than answering a question. Look for one thing changed and one thing measured.

quiz.p: What did a first cell need, as far as scientists can tell?
opts: A skin, copied instructions and energy
A heart, lungs and a brain
quiz.why: Every cell has a membrane, instructions that are copied, and a steady energy supply. Water is needed too, but water alone is not enough.

quiz.p: What warms the water of an alkaline vent?
quiz.why: Sea water reacts with olivine rock, and the reaction gives out heat. Melted rock is what heats a black smoker, so that choice mixes up the two kinds of vent.

quiz.p: Who makes the food at a deep-sea vent?
opts: Nobody, the animals do not eat
quiz.why: Bacteria and archaea make sugar using energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide. No light reaches the vent, so seaweed is not found there.

quiz.p: What can RNA do that makes the RNA world idea possible?
opts: Carry instructions and act as a catalyst
Make its own building blocks from air
Last for ever in hot water
quiz.why: RNA does both jobs that DNA and proteins share between them today. RNA does not last well in hot water, which is one of the idea's problems.

quiz.p: True or false: the RNA world idea has been proved.
quiz.why: False. There is good evidence, such as ribozymes and the RNA core of the ribosome. But nobody has made RNA that copies all of itself, and other scientists think simple reactions came first.

quiz.p: In very salty water, soap makes little foam. What does this suggest about the first cell skins?
opts: Simple fatty skins may form badly in sea water
The sea has no fatty molecules
quiz.why: Fatty acids behave like soap, and salt pushes them out of the water. This is an argument for fresh water pools. A later test showed that a mixture of fatty molecules can form skins in salty water.

quiz.p: Why are three bottles of the same size, shaken 20 times each, used in the foam test?
opts: So that only the salt differs
So that the foam looks nicer
Because three is a lucky number
So that the soap dissolves faster
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Then any difference in the foam must come from the salt.

quiz.p: A string of 100 centimetres stands for 4,500 million years. What is 1 centimetre?
quiz.why: 4,500 ÷ 100 = 45. Every centimetre stands for 45 million years.

quiz.p: On a model of Earth's history, for how much of the time was all life single cells?
quiz.why: Life is at least 3,500 million years old, and animals big enough to see appeared about 570 million years ago. So for more than four fifths of life's history there were only single cells.

quiz.p: How do scientists work out what LUCA was like, with no fossil of LUCA?
opts: From features that all living cells share
quiz.why: A feature shared by every branch of life was most likely inherited from the shared ancestor. So what all cells share tells us what LUCA had.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists agree that life began at vents.
quiz.why: False. Vents and pools on land are both leading ideas, with evidence for and against each. Nobody knows yet.

quiz.p: Which of these is known, and not just an idea?
opts: Fatty molecules form skins by themselves
Life began in a warm pool
quiz.why: Anyone can watch fatty molecules form skins, and it has been seen under microscopes many times. The other three are hypotheses that are still being tested.

applications: Space missions look for life on ocean moons such as Enceladus and Europa. Scientists choose where to look partly from ideas about where life began on Earth.
India's Deep Ocean Mission explores vents in the Indian Ocean. Vent chimneys hold metals, and the life around them is found nowhere else.
Microbes from hot springs make enzymes that still work when hot. One such enzyme is used all over the world to copy DNA in medical tests.
Some medicines and vaccines are made of RNA wrapped in tiny fatty bubbles. The bubbles form by themselves, as the first skins did.
Chemists design detergents so that salt and hard water do not push them out of the water. That is why dish liquid foams where bath soap fails.
Geologists, map makers and model builders all use scale. One unit on the model always stands for the same amount of the real thing.

spotted.art: A child at the edge of the sea rubbing a bar of soap between wet hands, with hardly any foam.

spotted.text: Borewell water in many Indian towns is hard. Soap forms a white scum in it and lathers poorly, for a reason close to the salt effect.
spotted.art: A steel bucket of water with a thin white scum on top and a soap bar on the rim.

spotted.text: At salt pans, sea water dries in the sun. The salt is left crowded together as crystals.

spotted.text: A hot spring, where water heated inside the rock comes up, as at a vent.

open_questions.q: How did the first cell begin?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made building blocks, RNA that does some jobs, and fatty bubbles that grow and split. Nobody has joined them into something alive.

open_questions.q: Where did life begin: at vents in the deep sea, in pools on land, or somewhere else?
open_questions.why_open: There is real evidence for both, and real problems with both. Almost no rock from that time is left to check.

open_questions.q: Did RNA come first, or did simple reactions come before any instructions?
open_questions.why_open: RNA can do two jobs, but it is fragile and hard to make. Nobody has yet shown RNA copying all of itself without help.

open_questions.q: How did a skin, a chain of instructions and an energy supply come to work together?
open_questions.why_open: Each has been studied alone. How the three first joined into one cell that could have young is the least understood step.

open_questions.q: Did life begin only once on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: All life today descends from one ancestor. Other beginnings may have happened and died out, leaving no trace we can find.

open_questions.q: Is there life on ocean moons such as Enceladus and Europa?
open_questions.why_open: They have liquid water and, probably, vents. No mission has yet been able to test their water for living cells.

What in our kitchen forms a skin by itself? Think of hot milk, dal and oil on water.
Your arm span is the age of the Earth. How long is your own life on that scale?
What do you share with the bacteria in curd? How do you know?
Why do you think life does not begin from nothing in a puddle today?
Would you trust an idea more if it was tested once, or tested by people who disagreed with it?
If we find cells on another world, what one thing would you check first?

jokes.j: Why did the soap refuse to go to the beach?
jokes.a: Too much salt. It could not get a good lather going.

jokes.j: What did the alkaline vent say to the acid sea?
jokes.a: There is a real difference between us. Let's put it to work.

jokes.j: Why was the long RNA chain so nervous?
jokes.a: Twelve letters, and someone was rolling dice.

jokes.j: What did the fatty acid say to the water?
jokes.a: I'm in up to my head. My tail is staying out of this.

jokes.j: Why did the black smoker never get invited to parties?
jokes.a: Everyone said the same thing: too hot, and far too much smoke.

jokes.j: How long did the single cells wait for animals to turn up?
jokes.a: About three billion years. Nobody had invented clocks, so nobody minded.

jokes.j: Why did the drying pool feel so popular?

jokes.a: Any family get-together. Everyone alive is on the guest list.

jokes.j: Why did the geologist stretch her arms out at the party?
jokes.a: Somebody asked how old the Earth was.

maths.problem: A string of 125 centimetres stands for 4,500 million years. How many million years is 1 centimetre? Oxygen began to build up in the air 2,400 million years ago. How far from the Today end does that label go?
maths.answer: 1 centimetre is 36 million years. The oxygen label goes about 67 centimetres from the Today end.
maths.explain: 4,500 ÷ 125 = 36, so each centimetre stands for 36 million years. Then 2,400 ÷ 36 is 66 and two thirds, which is about 67 centimetres. That is just past the middle of the string.
maths.context: This is about Deep Time on Your Arms. There a string as long as your arm span stands for the whole age of the Earth.
maths.why_maths: Dividing gives one fixed scale for the whole string. Without it, the labels would only be guesses.

maths.problem: The Earth is about 4,500 million years old. Write that number in digits. Humans like us have lived for about 300 thousand years. How many times older is the Earth than our kind of human?
maths.answer: 4,500,000,000. The Earth is about 15,000 times older than our kind of human.
maths.explain: 4,500 million is 4,500 followed by six zeros: 4,500,000,000. 300 thousand is 300,000. Cancel five zeros from both: 45,000 ÷ 3 = 15,000. So if all of Earth's time were 15,000 days, which is about 41 years, humans would have arrived on the last day.
maths.context: This is about Deep Time on Your Arms. There the first humans could not be marked with a ruler, because their part of the string was too thin.
maths.why_maths: Writing out the zeros and dividing shows how small a share of Earth's time is ours. The words 'million' and 'thousand' hide that.

maths.problem: In Copy or Crash, Lakshmi takes 36 turns with a 4-letter chain. Her copy is perfect 17 times. Then she takes 36 turns with a 12-letter chain. Her copy is perfect 4 times. How many points does each chain earn? Which length should she choose?
maths.answer: The 4-letter chain earns 68 points and the 12-letter chain earns 48 points. She should choose the 4-letter chain.
maths.explain: 17 × 4 = 68 points. 4 × 12 = 48 points. The long chain wins three times as much each time, but it wins far less than one third as often. So over many turns the short chain earns more.
maths.context: This is about the dice game Copy or Crash. There you roll once for each letter of an RNA chain, and any 1 spoils the copy. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A big prize that is rarely won can be worth less than a small prize won often. Multiplying shows which chain really does better.

maths.problem: Look at the table of foam heights. In each round, what fraction of the plain water foam did the sea-salty bottle make? In which round did the sea-salty bottle do best, compared with plain water?
maths.answer: One third in round 1, one third in round 2 and one half in round 3. The sea-salty bottle did best in round 3.
maths.explain: Round 1: 1 out of 3 is one third. Round 2: 2 out of 6 is one third. Round 3: 4 out of 8 is one half. With more soap added, the salt could not push all of the extra soap out of the water. So the sea-salty bottle began to catch up.
maths.context: This is about the Salt Water Skin Test. There you shake the same soap in plain, sea-salty and very salty water, and measure the foam. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: height of foam in centimetres

maths.why_maths: The heights alone all go up with more soap. Fractions show whether the salty bottle is falling behind or catching up.

maths.problem: Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in 1 litre. How much salt is that in a 200 millilitre tumbler? Your very salty bottle had 24 grams of salt in one tumbler. About how many times as salty as the sea was it?
maths.answer: 7 grams in one tumbler. The very salty bottle was a little more than 3 times as salty as the sea.
maths.explain: 200 millilitres is one fifth of a litre, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7 grams. Four level teaspoons of salt are about 24 grams. 24 ÷ 7 is a little more than 3.
maths.context: This is about the Salt Water Skin Test. There one level teaspoon of salt in a tumbler of water stood for sea water, and four teaspoons made very salty water.
maths.why_maths: The test only tells us about the sea if the salty bottle really is about as salty as the sea. Working out grams in a tumbler checks that.

maths.problem: Squeeze all 4,500 million years of Earth's history into one day of 24 hours. How many million years is one hour? The big dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago. About how many minutes before midnight is that?
maths.answer: One hour is 187.5 million years. The dinosaurs died out about 21 minutes before midnight.
maths.explain: 4,500 ÷ 24 = 187.5 million years in each hour. One minute is 187.5 ÷ 60, which is about 3.1 million years. 66 ÷ 3.1 is about 21 minutes. So on this clock the dinosaurs died out at about 11:39 at night.
maths.context: This is about Deep Time on Your Arms. There you made one scale model of Earth's history. Here you change the model from a length to a day.
maths.why_maths: The same history can be put on any scale. Changing the scale and getting matching answers shows that you understand the model.

warmup.q: What two jobs can RNA do?

warmup.q: Do scientists know where life began?
warmup.a: No. Vents in the sea and pools on land are the two leading ideas.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that life can live on chemical energy from rock, with no sunlight? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Until 1977, biologists thought the deep sea floor was almost empty. All food begins with plants, plants need light, and no light reaches the bottom. So deep-sea animals had to live on scraps sinking from above. On 17 February 1977, the geologists Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel went down 2,500 metres in the small submarine Alvin, near the Galápagos Islands. They were looking for hot springs in the rock. They found the springs, and around them crowds of large clams and other animals. There was not one biologist on the ship. What were the animals eating? About three years later, Colleen Cavanaugh, a new student at Harvard University, heard a talk about the giant tube worms from the vents. The worms have no mouth and no gut, and their bodies hold crystals of sulfur. She said that the worms must have bacteria inside them who feed on the sulfur chemicals in the vent water. She and her colleagues looked, and found the bacteria. Their report came out in 1981. Life could be built on energy from rock and water alone. Scientists then began to ask whether life had started that way.
how_we_found_out.who: Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel, geologists working in the United States, and Colleen Cavanaugh, an American biologist who was then a student
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That every food chain on Earth begins with sunlight, so the deep sea floor must be almost empty. The crowded vents, and the bacteria inside the tube worms, showed that food can also be made with energy from chemicals.
how_we_found_out.art: A small white submarine shining its lights on a crowd of large white clams around a shimmering crack in dark rock.

roots.context: We have learned how life might have begun, with a skin, a chain of instructions and a flow of energy. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Salt Water Skin Test, nobody built the foam. The soap molecules lined up into skins by themselves, and how well they did so depended on the water around them. Fatty molecules on the young Earth closed into hollow skins in the same way. So an inside and an outside can exist before anything is alive. The first cell did not have to build the first skin.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a skin or a wall as something a living being builds, to keep the world out. But the first skin was not built from the inside by anyone. The molecules and the water outside made it, and what the water held decided whether it could form at all.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Salt Water Skin Test, the same soap made tall foam in plain water and little in very salty water. In laboratories, fatty acids close into hollow bubbles that can hold RNA, grow and split. In 2018 such bubbles formed in hot spring water but not in sea water, and in 2019 a mixture formed them in salty, alkaline water.

three.who_am_i: Every cell of your body is wrapped in a fatty skin of the kind that forms by itself in water. Every cell also makes energy with a flow of protons, as LUCA did about four billion years ago.
three.what_is_life: A skin, a chain that can be copied and a flow of energy can each exist without life. Life may be what happened when the three began to work as one. Nobody knows yet how they joined.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth was not an empty stage waiting for life to arrive. Rock, sea water and heat carried out the first steps themselves. The chemistry of the water decided what could happen next.

roots.thread: Before there was life, there was one Earth of rock, water and air. Fatty molecules met water and arranged themselves into skins. Building blocks joined into chains, and some chains were copied. At some point a skin, a chain and a flow of energy became one cell. From that one beginning came every bacterium, tree, crow and person. The molecules that made the first skins already responded to water, to salt and to each other. Sensing begins with that kind of responding, so awareness did not have to arrive later from nowhere.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that in the beginning there was Being alone, one without a second. Some people say that in the beginning there was only non-being, and that being was born from it. But how could that be, Uddalaka asks. How could being come from non-being?
teachings.link: This is the unit's question, asked more than 2,500 years ago: can something come from what is wholly unlike it? The science so far finds no sudden jump. Skins, chains and energy flows were all present in the non-living world before the first cell.

teachings.teaching: Clay is shaped into a pot, but it is the empty space inside that makes the pot useful. Doors and windows are cut to make a room, but it is the empty space inside that makes the room useful.
teachings.link: A fatty skin matters because of the space it closes off. Inside that space, molecules could stay together long enough to work with each other. The skin made an inside possible.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, letter to Joseph Hooker, 1 February 1871
teachings.teaching: Darwin imagined life starting 'in some warm little pond', with ammonia, salts, light and heat. He added that today such matter 'would be instantly devoured or absorbed', which would not have happened before living creatures existed.
teachings.link: This is why life does not begin again in a puddle now. The living world that came from the first cells would eat any new beginning. Life changed the conditions that made it.

science.text: Every living cell today descends from one population of early cells.
Fatty molecules form closed skins in water by themselves, and such bubbles can grow and split in the laboratory.
How a skin, copied instructions and an energy supply first came together into a living cell.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, as reported in Madhava's Sarvadarshanasangraha, chapter 1
other_view.view: The Charvakas taught that there is only matter. Awareness appears when the elements are combined into a body, they said, just as the power to make people drunk appears when certain ingredients are mixed and left to ferment. In this view, the molecules before the first cell had no awareness at all. Many scientists today think something similar: that awareness needs a nervous system, and came billions of years after life began.

practice.title: The skin you live inside
practice.say: Sit still and rest one hand on your other arm. Feel your skin from the outside, and then from the inside. Breathe in slowly. Air that was outside you is now inside you. Breathe out. Every one of your cells has a skin as well, far too thin to feel. Each one is letting things in and out, right now. Sit for five more breaths. Notice that your edge is busy all the time.
practice.kid: Sit still. Rest one hand on your arm. Feel your skin from outside, then from inside. Breathe in slowly. Outside air is now inside you. Breathe out. Each of your cells has a skin too. Take five more slow breaths.

ask: Nobody built the foam in your bottle. Does order always need a maker?
A skin, a chain and a flow of energy are each not alive. When they work together, what has changed?
If the steps to life were already in rock and water, where would you draw the line between living and non-living?
Nobody knows how life began. How does it feel to live inside a question that is still open?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step for a city flat, with amounts and times. None has been tried at home yet, so a person should try the Salt Water Skin Test before families do. That test (core) needs a true bath soap bar. With a true soap, published classroom tests and long experience at sea agree that salty water gives less lather. With a detergent bar, liquid handwash or dish liquid, all three bottles may foam alike, and the step says what to do then. Hard tap water also lowers the foam in the plain bottle, so the step says to use drinking water. One level teaspoon of salt in a 200 millilitre tumbler is about 6 grams, close to the 7 grams that sea water would hold. Hot Vent in a Jar needs a grown-up for the hot water. Lower the bottle slowly, or the colour mixes at once. Use hot water, not boiling, so a cold glass bottle does not crack. Turmeric paper turns red-brown with baking soda water and with soap water, and it stains cloth. Drying Drops needs sun or a night indoors. Copy or Crash was checked by working out the chances: about 48 in 100 for 4 letters, 23 in 100 for 8 and 11 in 100 for 12, and about 71 in 100 for 12 letters with the checker. A game to 24 points takes about 12 turns for each player. The numbers in the made-up results agree across the experiment, the maths and the worksheets. Facts checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026: the Lost City discovery (date, people, towers, water, distance from the ridge), the 1977 vent dive, Colleen Cavanaugh's work, the ribozyme and RNA world dates, the 2009, 2016, 2018, 2019 and 2024 studies, Sudha Rajamani's wet and dry cycle work, the December 2024 Indian vent pictures, the Kairei depth, Darwin's 1871 letter and the Enceladus hydrogen report.
